Bestowing supreme glory, he has surpassed the Creator; casting away darkness, he has eclipsed the bearer of light (the sun);
dispelling the summer heat, he has conquered the beautiful moon—he is the Arhat here who is praised, for whom there is no equal. // 1.1 //

There was a city belonging to the great seer Kapila, situated on the lofty mountain peak which, with its vast and elevated splendor, had its flanks encircled like a row of clouds, and which was deeply embedded in the sky as if it were a high celestial mansion.
By its lofty manner, it surpassed the splendor of the clouds upon Mount Kailāsa;
and by carrying clouds that approached out of delusion, it rendered that very assumption fruitful.
In that city, which shone with the brilliance of the jewel-crystal (cratnaprabhā), darkness found no foothold as if it were poverty;
and Lakṣmī herself shone forth, as if smiling, because of her delight in dwelling there with the most excellent citizens. C 1.4 C.
In that glorious forest, the queen, perceiving that her time for childbirth had arrived,
took to a bed provided with a canopy, while being greeted with joy by thousands of women.
Then the constellation Puṣya became favorable, and from the side of that queen, who had been purified by her vows,
a son was born for the welfare of the world— without pain and without affliction.
Just as [the birth] of Aurva was from the thigh, that of Pṛthu from the hand, and that of Māndhātṛ— who was like Indra— from the head,
and likewise that of Kakṣīvat from the region of the shoulder, even so was his birth.
And he too, emerging from his mother’s womb like the sun from a cloud at dawn, made the world as bright as gold with his shimmering rays that dispelled the darkness. (1.26)
Then, as soon as he was born, the thousand-eyed Indra, filled with joy, gently took up that infant who was as fair as a golden pillar;
and from the sky there fell upon his head a shower of *mandāra* flowers along with two pure streams of water. // 1.27 //

Borne by those for whom the feet are the primary object of veneration, and coloring them with the networks of light-rays from his body, he surpassed in splendor the newly risen moon situated above the mass of twilight clouds. // 1.28 //
Having gradually emerged from the womb, he shone like one who had descended from the sky, not born through a birth canal,
as if after many eons.
He whose self was cultivated, who was fully conscious as he was born, and not deluded.
He shone with brilliance and composure (and with splendor),
like the young sun descended to earth; yet,
though so exceedingly radiant, he captivated the eyes of those who gazed upon him, just as the moon does.
For with the radiance blazing from his own limbs, he eclipsed the light of lamps like the sun;
possessing the beautiful hue of precious Jāmbūnada gold, he illuminated all the directions.

With steps that were unhurried, lotus-like, and free from confusion; rising up like a lotus, powerful like a crushing force, and characterized by long strides; likewise firm, he took seven steps and went forth like the constellation of the Seven Sages.
"I am born for enlightenment for the sake of the welfare of the world; this is my final birth in existence"—
thus looking toward the four quarters with the gait of a lion, he spoke these words which bring about the welfare of those capable of liberation.
Two streams of water, as white as moonbeams, flowing from the sky— one with a cool potency and the other with a warm—
fell upon his gentle head for the sake of providing unsurpassed physical comfort during his touch.
He was reclining upon a couch with a magnificent canopy and limbs radiant with gold, its feet made of lapis lazuli;
out of reverence for him, the lords of the yakṣas stood surrounding him, holding golden lotuses in their hands.
And by whose power the gods in the sky, with their heads bowed, held a white parasol over the son of Māyā, while they murmured supreme blessings for his enlightenment. (1.18)
The mahoragas, out of a thirst for the excellence of the Dharma and having performed their service under past Buddhas,
praised him with eyes distinguished by devotion and scattered mandārava flowers over him.

Delighted by the virtue of the Tathāgata’s appearance, the Śuddhāvāsa deities—beings of pure essence—rejoiced even though their own passion had vanished, for the sake of the world submerged in suffering. (1.20)
At his birth,
the earth, supported by the king of mountains as its stake, shook like a ship struck by the wind;
and a rain of sandalwood and the essence of blue and red lotuses fell from a cloudless sky.
Breezes blew, pleasant to the touch and delightful, causing celestial garments to fall;
the very same sun shone with increased brilliance, and the fire blazed with gentle flames even without being fanned.
And in the north-eastern part of the dwelling, a well with white water appeared of its own accord;
there, the women of the inner apartments, filled with wonder, performed their rites as if at a sacred bathing place.
The forest was filled by hosts of divine beings seeking the Dharma who came in great numbers to behold him;
and out of sheer curiosity, they offered flowers— even out of season— from their feet, along with fragrant blossoms.
And understand from us the illustrative examples in this regard. // 1.40 //
That treatise on statecraft which the two ancestral seers Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras did not compose,
O gentle one, was created by their sons, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, in the course of time.
Sārasvata also proclaimed the lost Veda, which those of old had not seen again;
likewise Vyāsa divided it into many parts, which the powerless Vasiṣṭha was unable to do.
Vālmīki was the first to compose verse, which the great seer Cyavana did not compose;
and that medical treatment which Atri did not perform, the seer Ātreya later proclaimed.
O King, that status as a twice-born which Kuśika did not obtain was attained by the son of Gādhi; and Sagara established the boundary at the ocean which the Ikṣvākus had previously failed to fix.
Janaka attained the status of teacher in the science of yoga— a position unattained by other twice-borns—
and as for those famous deeds of Śūra, even Śūra and the others were powerless to perform them.
Therefore, neither age, nor lineage, nor time is a criterion for superiority anywhere in the world;
for those various deeds of kings and sages were accomplished by sons, not by their ancestors.
Thus consoled and cheered by those trustworthy brahmins,
the king cast from his mind all unwelcome anxiety and ascended to even greater joy.
And being pleased, he bestowed wealth upon those best of the twice-born with due honor, saying:
"May this lord of the earth be as has been foretold; and when he reaches old age, may he go to the forests."
Then, having understood through signs and by the power of his asceticism that this was the birth of the one who would end the cycle of births,
the great seer Asita came to the palace of the Lord of the Śākyas out of a thirst for the true Dharma.

The king’s preceptor, with honor and hospitality, ushered that knower of Brahman— who was himself a knower of Brahman, blazing with the splendor of sacred knowledge and the splendor of asceticism— into the palace of the lord of men.
He approached the vicinity of the king's inner apartments, his heart overflowing with the surge of joy born from the birth of a prince.
The steadfast one entered [the city] as if under the impression that it were a forest, due both to the intensity of his asceticism and the onset of old age.
Then the king, having duly honored that sage seated upon his throne with water for the feet and the arghya offering,
invited him according to the prescribed rites, just as Antideva once invited Vasiṣṭha in the past.
"I am blessed; this family of mine is worthy of favor, since the Blessed One has approached desiring to see me.
Let it be commanded, O gentle one, what shall I do? I am your disciple; you may place your confidence in me. // 1.53 //
Thus addressed by the king with his whole being according to the facts, the Sage, his wide eyes blossoming with wonder, spoke these words, profound and steady.
This is worthy of you, a great-souled one, who are kind to guests, generous, and devoted to dharma—
that your affectionate mind should be thus disposed toward me, in accordance with my character, lineage, wisdom, and age.
And this was that by which those royal sages, having acquired subtle riches through dharma, [attained their goal].
Constantly renouncing according to the prescribed rule, they became rich in ascetic penances yet poor in worldly wealth.

Hear now the purpose for which I have come to you, and grant me your favor: on the celestial path, a divine voice was heard by me, saying that a son has been born to you for the sake of awakening. (1.57)

Having heard those words and applied my mind, and having understood through omens, I have therefore come here out of a desire to see the banner of the Śākya clan, which stands as high as the banner of Śakra.
Having heard these words, the king, his gait agitated by great joy,
took the prince— who was resting in the lap of his nurse— and showed him to the ascetic.

Then that great seer beheld the prince with wonder: his feet marked with wheels, his hands and feet with fingers and toes joined by a web, his eyebrows meeting at the brow, and his private parts enclosed in a sheath like those of an elephant.

Beholding him resting on the lap of the nurse as if he were resting on the lap of his mother, the son of Agni, his tears trembled within the lashes of his eyes; and sighing, he turned his face toward heaven.
Seeing Asita with eyes overflowing with tears, the king trembled out of affection for his son;
with a voice faltering and a throat choked with sobs, he questioned him.
With palms joined in reverence, his body bowed low.

O steadfast one, why do tears come to you upon seeing him—whose body differs but little from that of the gods, whose birth was most wondrous and radiant, and of whom you have declared the supreme future destiny? (1.63)
"O Blessed One, will the prince have a long life? Has he not been born for my sorrow?
Having somehow obtained this handful of water, will Time surely not come to drink it away? (1.64)
"Will my store of fame be imperishable? Will the core strength of my lineage remain secure?
And shall I go happily to the next world, even while my son—my one unblinking eye—is asleep? (1.65)
I fear that this sprout of my family has not yet blossomed and is destined for withering;
O Lord, tell me quickly, for I have no peace, since you surely understand the affection of kinsmen for their children.
Perceiving that the king was overcome with agitation by the thought of something undesirable, the sage spoke to him:
"O King, let there be no other thought in your mind; that which I have spoken is undoubtedly the truth. (1.67)
I have no agitation regarding any change in this [state]; rather, I am distressed by my own deception.
For time is passing for me, and he has been born who will understand the destruction of birth—a thing so difficult to attain.
Having abandoned his kingdom and become indifferent toward sense-objects, he will attain the ultimate reality through intense efforts;
for he shall blaze as a sun composed of wisdom to destroy the darkness of delusion in the world.

He shall rescue this world, which is being swept away by the ocean of suffering— with its foam of scattered diseases, its waves of old age, and its fierce current of death— by means of the great raft of knowledge. (1.70)

The world of living beings, tormented by thirst, shall drink from this supreme river of Dharma that has begun to flow—its current the force of wisdom, its embankment firm morality, its coolness meditative concentration, and its ruddy geese the religious vows. (1.71)

For he will proclaim the path to liberation to those afflicted by suffering, obscured by sense-objects, and standing on the trackless paths of the wilderness of *saṃsāra*, like to travelers who have lost their way. (1.72)
To people in this world who are being consumed by the fire of passion with sense-objects as its fuel,
he will provide refreshment with the rain of Dharma, like a great cloud with its rain at the end of the summer heat.

With the unsurpassed and unassailable mallet of the True Dharma, he shall shatter the door of living beings— the bolt of craving and the panels of the darkness of delusion— for the sake of their departure.

Having awakened for the sake of this world— which is enveloped by its own snares of delusion, overwhelmed by suffering, and without refuge— this King of Dharma will effect the liberation from bondage.
Therefore, do not feel grief on his account; rather, it is that person who is to be pitied in this world of men—
whether out of delusion, or through intoxication with the pleasures of desire— who shall not hear this dharma which leads to the ultimate goal.

Because I have fallen away from that virtue, even though I have attained the meditative absorptions, my purpose remains unfulfilled; for I consider that, due to not hearing that Dharma, even residence in the triple heaven is a calamity.
Having heard this meaning, the king, together with his friends and his wife, cast off all despondency and rejoiced;
thinking, "Such is this son of mine," he indeed considered even himself to be possessed of essential worth.
He made his heart subject to anxiety, thinking, "Will he indeed go by the path of the seers or that of the noble ones?
For it was not that he did not favor the side of the beloved Dharma; rather, he perceived fear regarding the destruction of his lineage.
Then the sage Asita, having declared the truth concerning the son to the king who was distraught for his offspring,
departed by way of the air just as he had come, his form watched with great reverence.
Having seen his daughter’s son and having considered both the sage’s words and her own disposition,
that virtuous man, out of compassion, directed him in many ways, as if he were his own beloved son.

The king also, delighted by the birth of a son, released those bound in prison who had fallen into misfortune, and performed for his beloved son all the rites appropriate to his lineage in the prescribed manner.
The birth-rite of the son. // 1.82 //
When ten days had passed, with a disciplined mind and filled with supreme joy, he performed prayers,
burnt offerings, auspicious rites, and worship of the deities for the highest welfare of his son.

Moreover, for the sake of his son's prosperity, he himself gave to the twice-born cows that were free from old age, yielding milk, adorned with golden horns, and accompanied by their calves which were firm, strong, and numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
Then, having performed various rites that pleased his own heart,
the self-restrained prince, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, joyfully set his mind upon entering the city.
Then, for the sake of her son’s welfare, the queen— having prostrated before the deities— ascended a costly palanquin made of ivory, adorned with white and pale flowers and lit by jeweled lamps.
Then, having caused his wife— who was accompanied by elderly women and protected by her infant son— to enter the city first,
the king also departed with the throngs of citizens, being honored like Maghavan by the immortals as he ascends to heaven.

Then, having entered the palace, the King of the Śākyas—rejoicing like Bhava at the birth of the six-faced Kārttikeya—his face filled with joy, performed various acts that brought prosperity and renown, exclaiming, "This! This! (1.88).
Thus, through the birth and growth of the king’s son, that city named Kapila, together with its countryside,
became as joyful at the birth of Nala (or Kūvara) as the city of Kubera was when filled with Apsarases.
[Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Birth of the Blessed One," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
From his very birth, that king— conqueror of himself— saw his son, who was destined to reach the end of old age,
increase day by day in wealth, elephants, horses, and allies, just as the ocean swells with the force of the waters.
Then indeed he obtained many treasures—of wealth and of various gems, as well as of wrought and unwrought gold—which were a burden even to his desires. (2.2)
Those Himalayan elephants, fierce with rut, who could not even be brought into this enclosure by lords of elephants resembling lotuses, approached him without any effort at all.

His city was agitated by horses— some adorned with various marks and new golden trappings, others unadorned, and still others with long manes— all acquired through his military power, his benevolence, and his wealth.
In his kingdom, there were many cows— well-nourished, contented, virtuous, free from dust, and yielding milk of excellent quality— who were accompanied by vigorous calves and yielded much milk. (2.5)
His enemy became neutral, his neutral kinsman turned into a friend,
and his ally attained particular firmness; while his other two factions met with destruction.
Likewise, there was for him the sound of gentle breezes and clouds, with the sky adorned by lightning as its earrings.
And at the proper time and place, the god sent down rain, free from the evils of falling stones, showers of dust, and thunderbolts.
The crops grew successfully and fruitfully according to the season, even with the labor of agriculture performed by him;
and those very same medicinal herbs [flourished].
They became even more distinguished by their flavor and their essence.
Even at that time, which threatened the very bodies [of women] as if the crush of battle had begun,
the noble ladies, by the power of Time, gave birth comfortably and healthily, remaining well-disposed and free from ailment.
Even when they possessed wealth that was censurable yet obtainable, men did not beg from others—except for those observing vows or those who were unable;
and even one who had only the smallest amount of property, being thus entreated, never turned away anyone at that time. (2.10)
In his kingdom, there was no one who lacked respect for elders,
nor one who failed to support kinsmen, nor one who was unobservant of vows, nor a liar, nor a violent man;
it was just as it was in the realm of King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.

And there, those who desired the Dharma performed rites for gardens, temples, hermitages, wells, water-stations, lotus-pools, and groves, as if they were perceiving heaven itself before their very eyes.
And the people, freed from the fear of famine and disease, rejoiced like those in heaven;
and neither wife transgressed against her husband, nor did the queen against her lord, each remaining faithful to the other.
No one pursued desire for the sake of pleasure; no one guarded wealth for the sake of desire;
no one practiced dharma for the sake of wealth; and no one committed violence for the sake of dharma.
His own realm, freed from enemies such as thieves and the like, became secure, prosperous, and free from foreign invasion;
and his cities and forests became peaceful and well-supplied with food.
Just as in the kingdom. // 2.15 //
For at that birth, in the kingdom of that king— just as it was in the reign of Manu, the son of Aditya—
joy prevailed, evil perished, righteousness blazed forth, and impurity was stilled.
Since such was the prosperity of that royal family and since his attainment of all aims had come to pass,
the king therefore gave his son the name Sarvārthasiddha.

But Queen Māyā, beholding the vast power of her son which was equal to that of the best of the gods, was unable to contain the joy she felt; she then departed for heaven [for the sake of his non-destruction]. // 2.18 //

Then his maternal aunt, whose power was equal to that of a mother, raised the prince— who was like the offspring of a god— with affection and devotion no different from her own, as if he were her own son.
Then that prince grew up properly and gradually, like the young sun standing at its rising, or like fire fanned by the wind, or like the lord of the stars in a cloudless fortnight.
Then, from the homes of their friends, they brought him highly precious sandalwood, strings of jewels filled with medicinal herbs, and golden chariots yoked with deer.
And ornaments suited to their respective ages, as well as golden elephants, deer, horses,
and chariots.
And [he gave] cows yoked with young bulls, as well as female calves adorned with gold and silver. // 2.22 //
Thus, being attended by those various objects of enjoyment suited to his age,
though he was but a child, he became like one who was not a child, distinguished by fortitude, purity, intellect, and splendor.
Having passed beyond childhood and having properly attained middle age at the appropriate time, that prince indeed undertook the practice of spiritual realization.
In a few days, he mastered those sciences appropriate to his lineage, which would otherwise require many years to master.

Having heard from the great seer Asita that his son’s future welfare would consist of the supreme good, the Śākya king generated an attachment to sensual pleasures [thinking], "He shall go to the forests"—[thus there would be prosperity for the King of the Śākya clan]. (2.25)

Then, from a family endowed with steadfast virtue, he took for him a virtuous wife named Yaśodharā—vast in fame and possessed of beauty, modesty, and discipline—who was like the goddess Śrī herself. (Or, according to another reading: "of equal renown. || 2.26 ||

Shining with a most excellent form, this prince, the beloved of the lord of the earth and a match for Sanatkumāra, took his delight together with that bride of the Śākya king, as the thousand-eyed Indra does with Śacī. (2.27)
Reflecting on how he might not see anything adverse that would disturb his mind,
the king assigned him a dwelling.
They [kept him] within the inner chambers of the palace itself, not allowing him to travel upon the ground.
Then, in palaces as white as autumnal clouds, shining like celestial chariots upon the earth—
mansions providing comfort in all seasons— he sported with noble music performed by women.
With mṛdaṅga drums bound with gold and struck by the fingertips of women,
and with dances equal to the performances of the most excellent apsarases, that palace shone like Mount Kailāsa.

There the women delighted him with their words, with graceful arts, with playful gestures, with amorous charms, with sweet laughter full of coquetry, and with the arching of their brows and sidelong glances. (2.31)
Then,
seized by women skilled in the arts of love and fierce in their passion,
he did not descend from the roof of the celestial chariot to the earth, just as one of meritorious deeds does not descend from the roof of a celestial chariot.
But the king, impelled by the desire for his son’s prosperity and by the destiny that was to come to pass,
delighted in tranquility, desisted from evil, practiced self-restraint, and shared his wealth with the virtuous.
He did not cling to the pleasures of desire like one who is fickle, nor did he feel improper passion for his mother;
with fortitude, he conquered his restless senses and horses, and he won over both his kinsmen and the citizens through his virtues.
He did not study knowledge for the sake of another’s suffering; rather, he mastered that auspicious wisdom which leads to bliss.
For just as he wished well for his own offspring, so too did he desire the welfare of all living beings.
He duly worshipped the radiant Aṅgiras, the presiding deity, for the sake of his son's long life;
he offered oblations into the non-faltering fire, and gave gold and cows to the twice-born.

He bathed his body to purify both mind and form with the waters of sacred fords and the waters of virtue; he drank the Soma prescribed by the Vedas and his own son, as well as the internal bliss of peace.
He spoke with conciliation, yet not in vain; he spoke what was true, yet nothing unpleasant.
For out of shame, he was unable to speak even to himself that which was conciliatory but untrue, or that which was harsh though true. (2.38)
Toward those things that were desirable and those that were undesirable, provided they required action, he did not fall into the state of being a locus for passion or hatred;
he practiced what was auspicious and pure in conduct, for he esteemed sacrifice not as it is commonly understood, but according to its true nature.
And he immediately quenched the thirst of one who approached him with hope by means of the waters he gave.
Except through battle, he did not split the arrogant pride of his enemies with his well-wielded axe.
He disciplined one [quality], he protected seven, he abandoned seven, and he preserved five;
he attained the threefold set, he understood the threefold set, he knew the twofold set, and he cast off the twofold set.

Even those who had committed offenses and were condemned to death, he did not cause to be executed, nor did he look upon them with anger; instead, he bound them with kindness and rewards, for even their release was seen by him as leading to no harm. // 2.42 //
He practiced the supreme vows of the seers; he cast off long-accumulated enmities;
he acquired glories fragrant with virtue, and he shed the dust that soils the soul.
He did not wish to seize an offering that had not been presented, nor did he desire to covet the property of others;
he did not wish to speak of the unrighteousness of his enemies, nor did he harbor anger in his heart.
When that lord of the earth had thus set himself in motion, his servants and citizens likewise moved in the same manner;
just as the senses of one engaged in yoga follow when the mind is tranquil and serene.
Then, in due time, to Yaśodharā— whose breasts were beautiful and who was truly worthy of the name— a son was born to Śuddhodana, whose face resembled that of Rāhu’s enemy; he was named Rāhula.

Then the protector of the earth, whose desire for a son had been fulfilled, was supremely delighted regarding the prosperity of his lineage; he rejoiced at the birth of his grandson just as much as he had rejoiced at the birth of his son.
"How might my affection for my son [or grandson] be directed toward him alone?"— with such thoughts, his joy having been kindled,
he who was fond of his son undertook various rites at the proper time, as if desiring to ascend to heaven.
Abiding on the path of the illustrious royal seers of the first eon,
he practiced austerities without casting off his white garments and performed sacrifices free from violence.
Then that man of meritorious deeds blazed forth, radiant with both royal splendor and the splendor of asceticism,
illuminated by his lineage, conduct, and intellect, like the thousand-rayed sun about to release its brilliance.

Having worshipped the *Arcika* hymn of Svayambhū, he— whose glory was firmly established— recited it for the sake of his son’s stability and performed difficult rites, like the Creator himself desiring to bring forth the worlds at the beginning of time.
He laid aside the sword and pondered the sacred scriptures; he cultivated tranquility and endured self-restraint;
like one who has mastered his senses, he did not pursue any object of desire; and like a father, he looked upon all objects with impartiality.
For he bore the kingdom for the sake of a son; he bore a son for the sake of the lineage, and the lineage for the sake of fame;
he bore fame for the sake of heaven, and heaven for the sake of his own self; and he desired the stability of his own self for the sake of dharma.

Thus he performed various religious rites, established by the virtuous through traditional usage and Vedic scripture, hoping and entreating: "Seeing what, would my son not go to the forest?"—how might my son remain? || 2.54 ||
On this earth, kings who desire to protect the royal fortune established within themselves guard their sons;
yet that lord of men, desiring righteousness, guarded his son from righteousness by releasing him from the objects of the senses.
All those Bodhisattvas of incomparable being, who knew the flavor of sensual pleasure and had fathered sons, went to the forest;
yet he, having accumulated karma, even though the cause was firmly rooted, pursued his delight until he attained awakening.
[Thus ends the second canto, named "The Pleasures of the Inner Apartments," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, on one occasion, he heard [the sounds] of groves adorned with lotus-pools, where the grass was soft and the trees resounded with the calls of male cuckoos, accompanied by songs.
He established those groves.
Then, having heard of the charming qualities of the city’s groves— which are so dear to women—
he set his mind on going outside, like an elephant confined within its stall.
Then the king, having heard the disposition of that wish called "son," ordered a pleasure excursion suitable for his affection, his prosperity, and his age.
And he caused the throng of distressed common folk on the royal road to turn back, thinking: "Lest the prince, whose mind is so delicate, become agitated in heart. (Civa) 3.4.

[He saw] monks who were deficient in their limbs, whose sense faculties were impaired, who were aged, afflicted by disease, and so forth, as well as those who were miserable, [scattered] in all directions.
Then, having cleared the way with the utmost gentleness, they brought about the supreme splendor of the royal road.
Then, when the magnificent royal road had been prepared, the illustrious prince, accompanied by humble attendants,
descended from the roof of the palace at the proper time and, having received permission, approached the king.

Then the lord of men, his eyes filled with tears, smelled the head of his son, gazed at him for a long time, and commanded him with his voice, "Go"; yet out of affection, he did not release him even in his mind.
Then he ascended a golden chariot, yoked with four quiet horses bearing ornaments of Jāmbūnada gold, which possessed pure rays like the light of a scholar’s intellect or a flash of lightning.

Then he reached the road, which was strewn with clusters of radiant flowers, hung with garlands, and adorned with fluttering banners; accompanied by a fitting retinue, he appeared like the moon amidst the stars traversing the sky.
As if being strewn with the exceedingly wide eyes of those filled with curiosity, which resembled half-open blue lotuses.
He proceeded slowly along the royal road, being gazed upon from all sides by the citizens.

Some praised him for his gentle qualities, while others worshipped him for his radiant splendor; some, because of his gracious countenance, perceived his majesty, and others wished him long life and great prosperity.
Hunchbacked women emerged from noble families, and troops of Kirātas and dwarfs;
women also came forth from humble dwellings, and like the banners of a divine procession, they bowed down.

Then, having heard from the servants the news that the prince was indeed departing, the women went to the rooftops of their palaces out of a desire to see him, having received permission from their honorable kinsmen.
Hindered by their slipping girdle-strings, with eyes agitated as if waking from sleep,
and having rearranged their ornaments, they surrounded him with unrestrained curiosity.
By the echoes from the floors of the palace stairs, by the sounds of their girdles, and by the tinkling of their anklets,
they terrified the flocks of domestic birds while jostling one another with their speed.
But as some of these excellent women hurried along with eager longing, their broad hips and full breasts, by virtue of their weight, checked their pace.

Although she was capable of moving quickly, another woman restrained her pace and did not go fast; bashful and concealing her ornaments— which were bold with beauty and had been applied for private dalliance— she proceeded slowly.
Then, as those women pressed against one another and crowded together, their earrings jingling and their ornaments tinkling, a tumultuous noise arose at the windows.
The lotus-faces of the women, with their earrings brushing against one another as they leaned out from the windows, shone like lotuses clinging to the palace walls.
Then the glorious city shone on all sides with palanquins borne by young women—their windows opened out of curiosity—like celestial chariots in the sky accompanied by *apsarases*. (3.20)
Because the windows were not wide, the faces of those most excellent women, with their earrings resting upon one another's cheeks, shone like clusters of lotuses tied together.

Beholding the prince on the road, the women appeared like those wishing to go to the earth; and the men, looking up at him with faces turned upward, appeared like those wishing to go to heaven. (3.22)
And having seen that prince, blazing with his physical form and splendor, those women softly said, "Blessed is his wife," with pure minds indeed and not from any other motive. (3.23)
"This man, indeed, with his long and muscular arms, is like the God of Love himself in visible form;
having abandoned worldly splendor, he shall attain the Dharma"—thinking thus, they showed him nothing but reverence. (3.24)
Seeing the royal road thus strewn with humble citizens of pure and resolute appearance, the prince rejoiced slightly and felt as if he were experiencing a second birth.
But the gods, dwelling in the pure realms, beholding that city as joyful as heaven itself,
fashioned an aged man in order to incite the son of the king to depart.

Then the prince, seeing him overcome by old age and his form distinct from that of other men, spoke to his charioteer with his gaze fixed steadily upon him: "Charioteer, what is this man who has come here, his appearance so different from that of other men?"

"O charioteer, who is this man who has approached us, with white hair and a staff held in his hand, his eyes hidden by his brows and his limbs slack and bent? Is this a transformation, or his natural state, or a mere accident? (3.28)
Thus addressed, the charioteer, his judgment deluded by those very gods, reported this matter to the prince—though it was something that ought to have been concealed—seeing no fault in it. (3.29)

The destroyer of beauty, the ruin of strength, the source of sorrow, the end of pleasures, the destruction of memories, and the enemy of the senses— this is what is called old age, by which he has been broken. (3.30)
For even he, as a child, drank milk; in time, he crawled further upon the earth;
having gradually become a handsome youth, he has in that same sequence arrived at old age.
When this had been said, the prince moved slightly and spoke thus to the charioteer:
"Will this same affliction befall me as well? Then the charioteer replied to him.
This excellence of youth will undoubtedly belong to the Venerable One as well through the power of time; thus the world both knows and desires that old age is the destroyer of beauty. // 3.33 //
Then that Great-Souled One, whose intellect was purified by his former aspirations and who had accumulated meritorious deeds throughout vast eons,
was terrified upon hearing of old age, like a bull hearing the roar of a great thunderbolt nearby.
Sighing deeply and shaking his head, fixing his gaze upon that aged man,
and seeing that very same crowd of people filled with joy, he spoke these words with deep agitation:
He spoke this. // 3.35 //
Thus old age strikes down all without distinction—memory, beauty, and prowess;
yet the world does not feel any sense of urgency, even while witnessing such things before its very eyes. (3.36)
"O charioteer, since this is so, turn back the horses; you must go quickly to our home.
For how can there be delight for me in the grounds of a pleasure garden when the fear of old age dwells within my mind? (3.37)
Then, at the command of that son of his father, the charioteer turned the chariot back;
thereupon the prince returned to that very palace, which, under the sway of anxiety, seemed to him as if it were empty.
But when he found no peace even there, examining it closely with the thought, "Old age, old age," he then,
with the permission of the king, went out once more by that same path in due course.
Then, the gods created another man whose body was overcome by disease;
and seeing him, the son of Śuddhodana, his gaze fixed intently upon him, spoke to the charioteer.
With a large belly, a body trembling from labored breathing, shoulders and arms drooping, and limbs thin and pale—
what man is this who, leaning upon another, utters the piteous word "Mother"? (3.41)

Then his charioteer said to him: "O gentle one, this is a great calamity called disease, which has arisen and increased from the disturbance of the bodily humors; by it even Śakra himself has been rendered powerless."
Having spoken thus, the prince, looking again at that man with compassion, said:
"He was born for this very purpose..."
This is a distinct fault; generally, there is fear of disease among living beings.
Then the charioteer replied: "O Prince, this affliction is common to all;
for even when tormented by diseases, people afflicted by pain still experience joy."

Having heard this meaning, his heart was despondent; he trembled like the moon reflected in the waves of water. Feeling compassion, he spoke these words in a somewhat gentle voice: iti śrutārthaḥ sa viṣaṇṇacetāḥ $ prāvepatāmbūrmigataḥ śaśīva & idaṃ ca vākyaṃ karuṇāyamānaḥ % provāca kiṃcinmṛdunā svareṇa // 3.45 //

Beholding this calamity of disease among living beings, yet the world continues to place its trust [in life]—alas for the ignorance of men! Those who have not been liberated from the fear of disease laugh. (4.46)
"Charioteer, let us turn back from this journey; let the chariot proceed only to the king's palace.
Having heard of the fear of disease, my heart, as it were, recoils, repelled from all pleasures. (3.47)
Then, having turned back with his joy departed, he entered his dwelling absorbed in deep reflection.
Having seen him thus twice turn back after his search, the lord of the earth made an inquiry regarding his arrival.
But having heard the omen of his return, he thought that the prince had abandoned himself;
and though enraged, he did not inflict severe punishment upon the official in charge of the road's clearing.
Furthermore, he ordained for that son a mode of life in the sensory realms that was endowed with special distinction.
Moreover, because he is subject to old age, he is not even capable [of staying]; thus, fearing that he might abandon us, we implore our Lord. (3.50)
And when his son took no pleasure at all in the objects of the senses, such as sounds and so forth, within the inner apartments,
he then ordered an excursion outside, thinking that there might be a different flavor [of experience] there. // 3.51 //
And out of affection, perceiving his son's disposition and disregarding certain faults such as passion and agitation,
he ordered that courtesans skilled in the arts and proficient therein be present there.
Then, on the royal road, which was especially well-adorned and inspected,
the king, having exchanged both the charioteer and the chariot, sent the prince forth outside.

Then, as the prince was proceeding in that manner, those very gods caused a corpse to be placed [before him]; and on that very road, the charioteer and the prince saw that dead man being carried along, and no one else.
Then the prince said to the charioteer: "Who is this being carried by four men, followed by wretched people, who, though adorned, is weeping? (Or: "Though adorned, he is weeping. 3.55.
Then, his mind overcome by those very gods of pure nature who dwell in purity, the driver spoke this matter— which was otherwise unspeakable— to the Lord, who knows the truth and possesses all power.
Though separated from the qualities of the intellect, the senses, and the vital breaths— sleeping, unconscious, and become like grass or wood—
he is [yet] cherished by those dear to him who protect him with great effort.
This something indescribable is being abandoned.
Having heard these words of the guide, he was somewhat agitated and said to him:
"Is this the dharma only for this single person, or is such an end common to all living beings? (3.58)
Then the Guide spoke to him: "This is the final deed for all living beings."
Whether base, middling, or great-souled, for everyone in the world destruction is certain. (3.59)
Then that son of a king, though steadfast, immediately despaired upon hearing of death; leaning his shoulder against the tip of the chariot pole, he spoke in a resonant voice:
60. Then that son of a king, though steadfast, immediately despaired upon hearing of death; leaning his shoulder against the tip of the chariot pole, he spoke in a resonant voice:

And yet this is the certain end for all creatures; the world is heedless and has cast off fear. I suspect the hearts of men are hard, for they remain at ease while traveling upon the road of life. (3.61)
Therefore, charioteer, let the chariot be turned back; for this is neither the place nor the time for recreation.
Knowing that destruction is certain, how could one who possesses consciousness remain heedless here at a time of such distress? (3.62)
Although the son of the king spoke thus, he did not turn back that chariot;
however, by the command of the lord of men, he drove forth specifically toward the forest where the lotus thickets grew.

Then he beheld that forest, auspicious with flowering young trees, filled with wandering, joyful, and intoxicated cuckoos, possessing beautiful long ponds like celestial chariots, resembling the Nandana grove itself. (3.64)
Then the prince was forcibly led (or brought) through that forest crowded with throngs of beautiful women,
like a sage newly bound by vows who, fearing obstacles, is led into the palace of the Lord of Alakā surrounded by excellent Apsarases.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Arising of World-weariness," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, from that city garden, women with eyes flickering with curiosity went out to meet the prince, as if to welcome a bridegroom who had arrived.
And having approached him, their eyes wide with wonder,
they performed the traditional rites of hospitality with hands resembling the buds of lotuses.
And they stood surrounding him, their hearts captivated by love,
as if drinking him in with their unblinking eyes that blossomed with joy.
For the women thought of him as Desire incarnate, adorned with radiant marks as if with natural ornaments. (4.4)
And because of his gentleness and steadfastness, some recognized him as the moon itself descended to earth with its rays concealed. (4.5)
Overwhelmed by his beauty, they yawned as if to seize him;
striking one another with their glances, they sighed softly.
Thus those women merely gazed at him with their eyes;
they neither spoke nor laughed, being restrained by his majestic power.
Seeing them thus devoid of activity and overwhelmed by love, the wise Udāyin, son of the family priest, spoke these words: (4.8)
"You all are masters of every art, skilled in perceiving the inner disposition; endowed with beauty and grace, you have attained preeminence through your own virtues. (4.9)
By these virtues, they would even outshine those Northern Kurus,
let alone this earth, which is the very playground of Kuvera.
You are capable of shaking even the sages who have transcended passion,
and you are able to capture even the gods when they are accompanied by celestial nymphs.
By means of your knowledge of dispositions, your gestures, your physical grace, and your beauty, you are capable of inflaming passion even in women; how much more so, then, in men? (4.12)
For you who are such as this, separated from your own proper sphere, such is your conduct; I am not pleased with your honesty.
This conduct of yours, with eyes downcast through modesty, would indeed befit young brides—or perhaps even cowherd women. (4.14)
"Even if this man were wise, illustrious, and great in power, one must reach the certain conclusion that even for women there is a great majesty; therefore, [the effort] must be made here. (4.15)
For in former times, the great seer Vyāsa—invincible even to the gods—was kicked by the foot of Kāśisundarī, a courtesan. (4.16)
In former times, the monk Manthālagautama, desiring to please the chief queen Vāraśālā, carried away her dead children for her sake. (4.17)
A woman, though inferior in both complexion and station, gratified the great seer Gautama Dīrghatapas, who was long-lived. (4.18)
In the same way, Śāntā captivated and carried off Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the son of a sage, who was inexperienced with women, by means of various stratagems. (4.19)
And the great seer Viśvāmitra, though he had plunged into profound austerity.
"Ten years he considered as a single day, while staying in the forest, having been captivated by the Apsaras Ghṛtācī. (4.20)
If such various sages as these were brought to transformation by women, how much more so the king’s son, who was in the prime of his youth and full of charm? (4.21)
This being so, therefore strive with confidence in such a way that this glory of the king’s lineage does not turn its back on this world. (4.22)
For those young women who captivate a person of equal status, yet grasp hold of the nature of both the inferior and the superior— those indeed are true women. 4.23.
Having heard these words of Udāyin, those women, as if pierced by arrows,
exerted themselves toward seizing the prince.
With their brows, glances, gestures, smiles, playful movements,
and gait, those women, as if terrified, made alluring gestures.
But by the command of the king and the gentleness of the prince,
they quickly cast off their reserve through intoxication and passion.
Then the prince, surrounded by a company of women, roamed through the forest like an elephant accompanied by a herd of females roaming the Himalayan woods.
Preceded by his women, he blazed forth in that delightful grove like the sun, surrounded by apsarases, shining in his celestial playground.
Some women there, overcome by intoxication,
touched him with their firm, full, and smooth breasts, which were pressed closely together.
Another woman, her tender vine-like arms weakly hanging down with drooping shoulders,
forcibly embraced him after making a false stumble.
One woman, with her copper-red lower lip and her mouth fragrant with wine, whispered into his ear: "Listen to a secret."
One woman, her body anointed with unguents, spoke as if giving a command:
"Offer your devotion here," desiring to clasp his hand [and thus touch him]. (4.32)
Another woman, whose blue garment slipped away under the pretext of intoxication again and again,
shone with her girdle visible like a night flashing with lightning.
Some wandered here and there with their golden girdles jingling, displaying to him their hips covered only by thin garments.
Others, grasping flowering mango branches, leaned forward,
displaying their breasts which resembled golden jars.
A certain lotus-eyed woman, having come from a lotus grove with a lotus in her hand,
stood by his side as he sat there like the goddess Padmaśrī beside the lotus-faced one.
A certain woman sang a sweet song, true to its meaning and accompanied by gestures, as if urging him—who was so composed—to wake up with her glances, saying, "You have been deceived. (4.37)
Another, with her beautiful face drawing back the bow of her eyebrows,
mimicked his movements with a steady and heroic grace.
A certain woman with full, lovely breasts and earrings swinging as she moved from the wind laughed loudly at him, saying, "May you find a mate! (4.39)
As he was thus departing, others bound him with garlands of flowers;
some seized him with the goads of their words, sweet yet full of reproach.
A certain woman, seeking a lover, took hold of a mango branch and, distressed by intoxication, asked: "To whom does this flower belong? (4.41)
One woman, assuming a masculine manner both in her gait and her posture, said to him: "Women have conquered you; O sir, conquer this earth! (4.42)
Then a certain woman, glancing about and smelling a blue lotus, addressed the prince with words slightly faltering from intoxication: (4.43)
"Behold, my lord, the mango tree covered with flowers fragrant as honey, where a cuckoo sings, confined within a golden cage. (4.44)
"Look at this Ashoka tree, which increases the grief of those who long for their lovers;
here the bees hum as if they were being scorched by fire. (4.45)
Behold the *tilaka* tree embraced by a mango branch, like a man dressed in white garments embraced by a woman with yellow unguents on her limbs. (4.46)
Behold the full-blown kurubaka flower, shining with the luster of rubbed-out red lac,
which seems to have bent down as if humiliated by the glow of women’s nails.
And look at this young *aśoka* tree, covered with new shoots,
which stands as if feeling ashamed because of the beauty of our hands.
Behold the long pond, covered with sinduvāra trees growing upon its banks,
like a young woman lying down, draped in a white silken garment.
Behold the greatness found even among women: for this ruddy goose follows his mate in the water from behind, attending her like a servant. (4.50)
"Listen to the sound of this intoxicated cuckoo as it cries; another cuckoo, right behind it, warbles like an echo, as if responding to the call. (4.51)
Indeed, the intoxication of passion is brought about by spring even for birds;
but it is not so for a person who fancies himself wise, whose mind dwells on the inconceivable.
Thus those young women, their minds made wild by love,
approached the prince with various such stratagems.
Though thus being provoked, he—his senses shrouded by fortitude—felt agitation at the thought that he must die; yet he neither rejoiced nor was he distressed.
Seeing their lack of stability in reality, that Supreme Person,
with a mind both deeply agitated and steadfast, reflected in his heart.
Do women not understand that youth is fickle, since they are intoxicated by their beauty, unaware that this very old age will eventually overtake them?
He will destroy it.
Surely these women do not perceive the onset of disease for anyone;
thus they are joyful, having cast aside fear in a world whose very nature is sickness. (4.57)
And clearly unaware of death, which carries away everything, they remain at ease and free from anxiety, playing and laughing. (4.58)
For what conscious person, knowing of old age, disease, and death,
would remain standing, sitting, or lying down at ease?
How much less, then, should one laugh? 4.59.
But he who, having seen another who is aged, diseased, or even dead, remains unperturbed and stays at ease—such a person is indeed one whose mind is like that of a brute beast. (4.60)
For when a tree is being separated from its flowers and fruits, or when it falls or is cut down, another tree does not grieve. (4.61)

Seeing him thus devoted to meditation and devoid of longing for sense-objects, Udāyin, who was learned in the treatises on policy, spoke to him out of friendship: iti dhyānaparaṃ dṛṣṭvā viṣayebhyo gataspṛham | udāyī nītiśāstrajñas tam uvāca suhṛttayā || 4.62 ||
"I have indeed been given to you as a worthy friend by the king; it is because of that affectionate regard that I desire to speak with you. (4.63)
Preventing one from what is harmful, encouraging engagement in what is beneficial, and not abandoning one in times of misfortune—this is the threefold characteristic of a friend. (4.64)
Thus, having pledged myself to loving-kindness, I turned my back on the goals of human endeavor.
If I were to neglect you, there would be no friendship on my part. (4.65)
Therefore, acting as a friend, I say this to you: such discourtesy toward women is not befitting of one who is young and handsome. (4.66)
It is even proper to comply with women by means of falsehood, for the sake of avoiding their shame and for the sake of one's own pleasure. (4.67)
Humility and compliance are the bonds for the hearts of women; for they are the source of affection, yet women desire honor. (4.68)
Therefore, O large-eyed one, even though my heart is turned away, you ought to comply with courtesy that is worthy of this beauty of yours. (4.69)
Courtesy is the medicine of women; courtesy is their supreme ornament. Beauty devoid of courtesy is like a forest without flowers. (4.70)
Or rather, let there be acceptance out of mere courtesy; let it be through affection.
Having obtained these objects so difficult to find, you ought not indeed to treat them with contempt.
Knowing that desire is supreme, even the god Purandara in former times lusted after Ahalyā, the wife of the sage Gautama.
Agastya requested Rohiṇī, the wife of Soma;
therefore,
according to sacred tradition, he obtained Lopāmudrā, who was her very likeness.
And [he was born] of Mamatā, the wife of Utathya (the son of Utathya), [he who was] of great asceticism.
Bṛhaspati begot Bharadvāja upon Mārutī.
And while Bṛhaspati’s queen was offering oblations,
the Moon— the best among those who offer— begat Budha, whose deeds were divine.
And in former times, on the bank of the Yamunā, Parāśara, having conceived passion, approached the maiden Kālī, who was born from the waters.
Out of a desire for dalliance with the despised Mātaṅgī Akṣamālā, the sage Vasiṣṭha begot a son, Kapiñjalāda. (4.77)
And even though his youth had passed away, the royal seer Yayāti took delight with the Apsaras Viśvācī in the Caitraratha forest.
Although the Kuru prince Pāṇḍu knew that association with women ends in destruction,
he was captivated by the beauty and virtues of Mādrī and indulged in the pleasure born of desire.
And Karālajanaka, having abducted the Brahmin’s daughter, met with ruin; thus one should not abandon the god of love. (4.80)
In this way, great souls such as these enjoyed even objects of sense that were censurable for the sake of pleasure, let alone those endowed with excellent qualities.
But you, moreover, being powerful, handsome, and young, yet reject through reason those sense-objects which this world is attached to. (4.82)
Having heard his words, which were gentle and consistent with the scriptures,
the prince, whose voice was like the rumbling of thunderclouds, replied:
These words of yours are fitting and reveal your affection;
yet, I shall persuade you regarding that point concerning which you hold me in such high regard.
I do not despise sense objects; I know that the world is composed of them.
Yet, considering the world to be impermanent, my mind finds no delight in this.
If these three—old age, disease, and death—did not exist, then even for me there would be delight in attractive sense-objects. (4.86)
Even if the bodies of women were always to remain exactly like this, my mind would not find pleasure in sensual desires— which, though they appear attractive, are full of defects. (87)
But when their beauty has been swallowed up by old age and becomes even to themselves undesirable, they would still take delight in it through delusion. (4.88)
Though subject to death, disease, and old age, he nevertheless took delight with those whose very nature was death, disease, and old age;
remaining unperturbed, he was no different from the beasts and birds.
As for what you said— that even those great souls were possessed by desire— no sense of revulsion should be felt toward them, since even they reached their end right here. (4.90)
I do not consider that to be greatness wherein there is general decay, or attachment to sense objects, or a lack of self-possession through disciplined practice. (4.91)
As for what you said—that one should deal with women even by means of falsehood—I do not recognize any such thing as falsehood, even when it comes to courtesy. (4.92)
And that compliance of mine is not pleasing where there is no uprightness; if there is no association with the whole being, then fie upon it! 4.93.
For one who is unsteady and untruthful, yet full of faith, attached, and seeing no fault— what indeed could there be to deceive a mind in which passion has arisen? (4.94)
If those who have conceived passion thus deceive one another, is it not indeed improper for men to look at women, or for women to look at men? (4.95)
This being so, [one should pity] one who is afflicted by suffering and subject to old age and death.
You ought not to entice me toward ignoble sensual pleasures.

"Aha! How exceedingly firm and powerful is your mind, you who perceive substance in fleeting desires! Even while observing all creatures on the path to death, you cling to sense-objects that bring even the most intense fear. (4.97)
I, however, am fearful and exceedingly distressed, brooding over the terrors of old age, calamity, and disease;
I find neither peace nor steadfastness, much less any delight, beholding the world as if it were ablaze with fire.

I consider the consciousness of that man to be made of iron, who, knowing for certain that death exists, yet conceives passion in his heart; he who does not weep but rejoices in the face of such great terror.
Then the prince delivered a discourse characterized by certainty, which destroys the foundation of desire;
meanwhile, the sun, its orb visible to the eyes of men, went to the mountain of setting.

Then those women, their ornaments and garlands worn in vain, and their artistic skills and endearments rendered fruitless, returned to the city with their hopes shattered, having restrained their passion within their own hearts.
Then, having observed the splendor of the people gathered in the city gardens withdrawn once more at evening,
the prince, reflecting upon the universality of impermanence, entered his palace.

Then, having heard that his mind was averse to the objects of the senses, the king could not sleep that night; with a dart lodged in his heart like an elephant, he and his ministers, exhausted by deliberating on many various paths, saw no other means of restraining the son’s inclination toward sensual pleasures.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Frustration by Women," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*. Then,
although being thus enticed by the most alluring objects of the senses,
the son of the Śākya king—
He found neither steadfastness nor peace; he was like a lion in his heart pierced by a deeply poisoned arrow.
Then, once accompanied by the sons of ministers— men who were capable, his friends, and skilled in varied conversation—
and desiring peace while longing to see the forest lands, he set out abroad with the permission of the king of men.

Having mounted his noble steed Kaṇṭhaka, which was equipped with a bridle of new gold and tinkling bells, and adorned with beautiful golden trappings and waving chowries, he set forth like the Lord of the Lotus-Tree (Brahmā) ascending his celestial vehicle.
Out of a longing for the forest and a desire for its virtues, he went to a region of the woodland that was even more remote.
And he saw the earth being ploughed, its furrows appearing like the transformations of waves upon the water.

Having observed the earth in such a state— its young grass and *darbha* blades torn up and scattered by the plow, and strewn with tiny insects, worms, and creatures— he felt as if he were witnessing the slaughter of his own kin.
He grieved intensely. // 5.5 //

Beholding the men plowing, their complexions marred by wind, sun, and dust, and seeing the draft-animals distressed by the exhaustion of drawing the load, the Supreme Noble One felt the highest compassion.

Then, descending slowly from the back of his horse, overcome with grief, he wandered over the earth; searching for the origin and passing away of the world, he spoke in distress: "Alas, this is indeed miserable! (5.7)

Desiring solitude in his mind, he turned back those friends who were following him and went to the foot of a rose-apple tree in a secluded spot, which possessed beautiful leaves that shimmered and quivered on all sides.
He sat down upon a spot of ground that was pure, strewn with fallen leaves, and covered with a carpet of grass as bright as lapis lazuli; there,
reflecting upon the origin and passing away of the world, he took hold of the path for the stability of the mind.

Having immediately attained stability of mind and being freed from the afflictions such as the desire for sense objects, he reached the first dhyāna— which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, is peaceful, and is of an untainted (anāsrava) nature.

Then, having attained the supreme joy and bliss born of seclusion—the concentration of the mind—he thereafter applied his attention to this very thing, having correctly observed the course of the world with his mind. (5.11)
Alas, it is a piteous thing that a person, being himself powerless and subject to the nature of disease, old age, and destruction, [should act thus].
The ignorant man, blinded by intoxication, feels revulsion toward one who is afflicted by old age, sick, or dead. // 5.12 //
If, being such as I am myself, I were to feel loathing for another who is of such a nature, that would be neither fitting nor appropriate for me, who understands this supreme Dharma. (5.13)

As he thus contemplated, according to reality, the defects of disease, old age, and calamity pervading the world—occurring within the course of strength, youth, and life—the pride residing within himself vanished in an instant. (5.14)
He neither rejoiced nor did he grieve; he fell neither into doubt nor into sloth and sleep;
he was not attached to the qualities of sensual pleasure, nor did he feel hatred, nor did he despise another. (5.15)
Thus this stainless and pure intellect grew within that great-souled one;
and while he was not being observed by other men, a man dressed as a mendicant approached him.
The son of the god among men questioned him: "Tell me, who are you? He then replied to him:
"O bull among men, fearing birth and death, I am a wandering ascetic who has gone forth for the sake of liberation. (5.17)

In this world subject to decay, I, seeking liberation, search for that auspicious and imperishable state; regarding my own kin and strangers as equal, with a mind unlike that of ordinary people, I have turned away from sense objects, free from passion and hatred. (5.18)
Dwelling anywhere— at the foot of a tree, in a deserted shrine, on a mountain, or in a forest—
I wander without possessions and free from desire, a mendicant receiving alms as they come, for the sake of the ultimate truth.
Having spoken this while the prince was looking on, he leapt up into the sky;
for that inhabitant of heaven, seeing him as one whose awakening was different from others, had come to him for the sake of his remembrance.
When he had gone into the sky like a bird, that best of men rejoiced and was filled with wonder;
and having then attained the perception of Dharma, he set his mind upon the method of renunciation.
Then he, equal to Indra and having conquered his senses and horses, desiring to enter the city, mounted the horse; yet,
looking back at his retinue of people, he did not proceed even then toward the forest he had desired.
Desiring to bring about the end of old age and death, he fixed his mind upon dwelling in the forest;
he entered the city once more not out of desire, but like a lordly elephant returning from the forest tracts to its enclosure.
"Happy indeed,
and truly at peace, is that woman whose husband is such as you, O long-eyed one!"—
thus the princess spoke with joined palms to him as he entered upon the road, gazing up at him. (5.24)
Then he of the voice like a great cloud heard this cry and attained supreme peace;
for having heard the word "extinguished," he set his mind upon the manner of final Nirvana.
Then he whose stature was like the peak of a mountain of gold, whose arms, voice, and eyes were like those of an elephant, a cloud,
and a bull respectively, who felt passion for the imperishable Dharma despite the decay [of the world], and whose face and prowess were like the moon and a lion, arrived there.
Then, with the gait of a king of beasts, he approached the monarch who was being attended by his circle of ministers,
like Sanatkumāra approaching Maghavan blazing in the assembly of the Maruts in the third heaven.
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he spoke: "O god among men, grant me graciously your permission;
I wish to go forth into the religious life for the sake of liberation, for separation is indeed certain for all people. (5.28)
Having heard these words of his, the king trembled like a tree struck by an elephant;
taking him by his lotus-like joined palms, he spoke these words with a throat choked with tears.
"Withdraw this resolve, my son; for this is not the time for you to take refuge in dharma.
In the first stage of life, while the mind is still fickle, they say that the practice of dharma is fraught with many faults. (5.30)

The mind of a youth, whose senses are curious about sense-objects and whose resolve is incapable of enduring the hardships of vows, wanders away from the forest—especially so for one unacquainted with discernment. (C: especially regarding non-discernment). 5.31.
But for me, O lover of dharma, it is now the time for dharma, having entrusted the royal fortune to you who are its worthy recipient;
O you of steadfast valor, through such valor dharma is maintained, but for you to abandon your father would be unrighteousness.
Therefore, abandon this resolve; for now, be devoted to the duties of a householder.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of youth, entry into the forest of asceticism is indeed delightful. // 5.33 //
Having heard these words of the king, he whose voice was like that of a sparrow replied:
"O King, if you will be my guarantor for four things, I shall not resort to the forest of asceticism. (5.34)
"May my life not be subject to death; may this health of mine remain free from disease; may old age not seize my youth; and may misfortune not take away this prosperity. (5.35)

To his son, who had thus spoken of this difficult-to-attain goal, the King of the Śākyas addressed these words: "Abandon this exceedingly lofty resolve directed toward such a course; for one whose desires exceed their bounds becomes an object of ridicule and is subject to failure. (5.36)
Then Meruguru said to his teacher: "If this course is not possible, I am not to be restrained;
for it is not right to hold back one who desires to escape from a house being consumed by fire."
Since separation from the world is inevitable,
it is surely better for one to separate oneself voluntarily rather than [be separated] by fate.
Surely death will forcibly separate me while my purpose remains unfulfilled and I am still unsatisfied. (5.38)
Having heard these words of his son who desired liberation, the lord of the earth,
declaring "He shall not go," once more established guards and provided him with the finest sensual pleasures.
But having been duly instructed by his ministers out of great respect and affection according to the scriptures,
and having been restrained by his father with tears, he then entered his residence, grieving.

He was gazed upon by women with tremulous eyes, like young does, whose faces were kissed by swaying earrings, whose breasts quivered with heavy sighs, and who looked up at him with longing glances. (5.41)
For he, bright as a mountain of gold and maddening the hearts of beautiful women,
captivated their ears, limbs, eyes, and souls by means of his voice, touch, form, and virtues.
Then, on the following day, blazing with his physical form like the sun, he ascended the palace as if to dispel the darkness with his own radiance, like the rising sun ascending Mount Meru.

Having ascended a magnificent golden throne, variegated with diamond inlays, which was like a tree of lamps blazing with the brilliance of gold and whose interior was filled with the incense of choice black aloe-wood, he took his seat.
Then, at night, the most excellent women approached him with musical instruments— he who was like Indra—
just as the throngs of Apsarases attended upon the son of the Lord of Wealth on the peak of the Himalayas, white as the moon.
Even with those celestial instruments as if they were divine, he found neither delight nor joy;
for that virtuous man, desiring to go forth toward the ultimate happiness of the supreme goal, took no pleasure in them.
Then, having perceived his resolve there by the Akaniṣṭha gods, who were preeminent in asceticism,
they simultaneously brought sleep upon the women and caused their bodily movements to become distorted.
For there, one woman lay down, resting her cheek upon her trembling hand;
she had left her lute—which was like a beloved wife, variegated with golden plates—lying in her lap as if in a fit of anger.
Another lay there with her flute held in her hand, her white garment slipping from her breasts;
she shone like a river whose banks laugh with water-foam, and whose lotuses are frequented by rows of straight bees.

As before, she slept embracing the mṛdaṅga drum with her two arms— as if embracing her beloved— arms that were as tender as the interior of a fresh lotus and adorned with armlets as brilliant as refined gold.
Others, adorned with ornaments of fresh gold and wearing unsurpassed yellow garments,
fell down helpless with deep sleep, like branches of the *karṇikāra* tree broken by an elephant.
Another lay leaning against the side of a window, her slender body bent like a bow; with her beautiful necklace hanging down, she shone like a carved statue on a gateway.
The lotus-face of another woman, bent down with its decorative leaf-patterns bitten by her jeweled earrings,
shone like a hundred-petaled lotus whose stalk is curved at the end and stirred by a standing kāraṇḍava bird.
Others, lying down just as they had been sitting, their bodies bent low by the weight of their breasts,
shone as they embraced one another with the nooses of their arms adorned with golden bracelets.
And a certain woman, embracing her large lute as if it were a female companion, lay fast asleep;
she rolled about with her golden strings trembling, her face agitated by its loosened cord yet radiant with its earrings.
Another young woman lay down, having placed a small drum— its beautiful cord not yet slipped from her shoulder—
between her thighs like a lover exhausted at the end of amorous play, as she rested with languid grace.
Others, though possessed of large eyes and beautiful brows, shone with their eyes closed;
they were like lotus-beds whose buds have closed at the setting of the sun.
Another lay there with her hair disheveled and loose, her ornaments and garments fallen from her hips,
and her necklaces scattered about, like a statue of a woman toppled over by an elephant.
But others, helpless and stripped of shame— though possessed of fortitude and endowed with the excellence of their physical forms—
lay there breathing heavily, distorted and cast down.
And their arms yawned. // 5.59 //
Others, with their ornaments and garlands cast aside, their garments disarrayed and loose, were unconscious;
with their white eyes unblinking and motionless, they lay there like those whose life-force had departed, lacking all splendor.
With her mouth wide open, her limbs distended, saliva falling from her jaws, and her private parts exposed,
another lay as if reeling with intoxication; she did not speak,
yet she maintained a distorted form.
Thus, that company of women, lying down in various postures according to their respective natures and lineages,
bore a resemblance to a lake whose lotuses have been bent and broken by the wind.
Having observed those young women lying there in such a state— distorted and lacking self-control—
the prince, though possessed of a virtuous body and lovely speech, felt a sense of revulsion toward them.
In this world of living beings, such is the impure and distorted nature of women;
yet, deceived by garments and ornaments, a man conceives passion for the objects of women. (5.64)

If a man were to reflect upon the nature of women and such transformations as these which are like a dream, he would certainly not increase his negligence in this matter; yet, struck down by the mental construction of their virtues, he falls into passion.
When he perceived this interval, the desire to depart at night arose within him; then, having understood his thought, the gods opened the door of the palace for him.
Then he descended from the roof of the palace, reproaching those young women as they lay asleep;
having descended, he went forth without hesitation through the first courtyard of the house.
Having awakened his swift groom Chandaka, who was attending to the horses, he spoke to him thus:
"Bring the horse Kanthaka with haste; today I desire to go from here to attain the deathless."
The satisfaction that has arisen in my heart today, and the resolve that has taken root in my mind,
as well as the fact that even in this solitude I feel as if I have a protector— surely the goal I desire is close at hand.

"Since these young women have cast aside both modesty and deference and lie before me as if unconstrained, and since the door-panels have opened of their own accord, surely the time has now come for me to depart for my own welfare. (5.70)
Then, having received his master’s command, although he already understood the king’s decree,
as if urged by another within his own mind, he set his thoughts upon bringing back the horse.

Then he brought that excellent horse to his master— a horse whose mouth was filled with a golden bit, whose back was covered with a light bedding, and who was endowed with strength, courage, and speed.
With his heels, the base of his tail, and his haunches spread wide; with his tail, back, and ears held close and short;
with his back, belly, and flanks alternately depressed and elevated; and with his broad muzzle, forehead, hips, and chest.
Embracing him, that broad-chested man comforted him with a lotus-like hand and instructed him with words of sweet syllables, as if desiring to enter the midst of an army.
"Indeed, many enemies (namely the Kali-enemies) have been repelled in battle by the king after mounting you;
I too [shall attain] the immortal state (the supreme goal)."
O best of horses, act in such a way that I may obtain it exactly as it is.
Companions are indeed easy to find in battle, or in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, or in the acquisition of wealth;
but for a man fallen into calamity or seeking refuge in the Dharma, companions are difficult to find.
And those who here become my companions— whether in a foul deed or in reliance upon dharma— as my inner self perceives it, those people will certainly share in the fruit thereof. (5.77)
Having understood this, my departure from here— which is joined with the Dharma—
for the welfare of the world,
O best of horses, strive with speed and valor for your own benefit and for the benefit of the world.
Having thus instructed his excellent steed in its duty, as if advising a friend, the best of men, desiring to go to the forest, ascended it—
his body radiant and possessing the luster of the dark-traveling moon— as the sun mounts an autumnal white cloud.

Then that noble steed, avoiding any sound that might wake his attendants in the fierce midnight, went forth with his jaw-noises silenced and his neighing stilled, his paces broken and released with cautious steps.
Then the Yakṣas, their bodies bent low, supported his hooves with the tips of their hands— hands whose forearms were adorned with golden bracelets and which, like lotuses,
seemed to pluck them from the earth as they moved with startled steps.
Those city gates, which were closed with heavy crossbars and doors and could not be opened even by elephants at their ease,
became open of their own accord before the prince as he passed, their sounds silenced.

Having resolved his mind and become indifferent to all things, he then departed from his father’s city, leaving behind his father who stood before him, his young son, his devoted people, and unsurpassed royal splendor.
Then he, whose eyes were like the petals of a stainless, blooming lotus, looked toward the city and let out a lion’s roar:
"I shall not enter this city again until I have seen the further shore beyond birth and death."
I have entered [the city] named Kapila.
Having heard these words of the Lord of Wealth, the hosts of his assembly rejoiced;
and the throngs of gods, with hearts full of joy, wished him success in his resolve to break his fast.
Other gods, whose bodies were like fire, having learned of his resolve— which was exceedingly difficult and hard to perform—
acted [to assist him].
On the path, there was light, like moonbeams streaming through the gaps in thick clouds.
The sky was harsh with the glow of dawn; he traveled many *yojanas* through the atmosphere. // 5.87 //
Thus ends the fifth canto, named "The Great Departure," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, when the sun— the eye of the world— had risen for a short while,
that best of men beheld the hermitage of Bhārgava.
Seeing that place where the deer slept in confidence and the birds remained at ease,
he felt as if he had found rest and as if his purpose were fulfilled.
To dispel their astonishment, for the sake of ascetic merit and worship,
and to maintain his own self-restraint, he descended from the back of the horse.
Having dismounted, he touched the horse, saying "It is crossed," and spoke to Chandaka with joy, as if bathing him with his eyes.
"O gentle one, by pursuing this horse with a speed like that of Tārkṣya,
you have demonstrated your devotion to me and your own prowess."

In every way, even though I am occupied with other duties, I have been grasped by you within your heart; for such is this love for a husband that you possess, and it is indeed capable [of such devotion].
One who is capable yet lacks affection exists; one who possesses devotion yet lacks capability also exists;
but one who is both devoted and capable, such as you, is rare indeed upon this earth.
Therefore, I am pleased with this noble deed of yours, in which such devotion toward me is seen, even while you turn your back upon the fruits of action.
Who would not stand face-to-face with a person who has attained success?
Even one's own kin mostly turn into strangers when misfortune strikes.
A son is maintained for the sake of the family; a father is served for the sake of support; the world clings together out of expectation—there is no such thing as self-interest without a motive.
What is the use of speaking at length? In brief, I have done what is most greatly pleasing to you.
Turn back, taking the horse; I have reached the desired place, the forest.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one, desiring to bestow his favor,
removed his ornaments and gave them to him whose mind was distressed.
Taking from his crown a brilliant jewel that illuminated the diadem and performed its function,
he stood uttering these words, like Mount Mandara with the sun.
With this gem, O Chanda, the king, having bowed down many times, should be petitioned with full confidence for the sake of relieving his anguish. (6.14)
I have entered this grove of asceticism for the sake of destroying birth, old age, and death;
certainly not out of a thirst for heaven, nor from a lack of affection, nor out of anger.
Therefore, since he has thus departed, you ought not to grieve for me;
for even after a long time of union, that union shall cease to exist in the course of time.
Since separation is inevitable, my mind is set upon liberation; how might I never again experience parting from my own kin and others? (6.17)
"You should not grieve for me, who have gone forth to abandon sorrow;
