rather, those impassioned ones who are attached to sensual pleasures—the very causes of grief—are the ones to be pitied. (6.18)
"And this, it is said, was the firm resolve of our ancestors; therefore, as one following the path that has become my inheritance, I am not to be grieved for. (6.19)
For upon the passing of a man, those who inherit his wealth become the heirs to his property;
but heirs to his Dharma on this earth are rare, or perhaps do not exist at all. (6.20)
Even if it should be that he has gone to the forest at an improper time, there is no such thing as an "unseasonable" time for the Dharma when life is so flickering. (6.21)
"Therefore, my resolve is this: I must seek my own welfare this very day.
For what confidence can there be in life while death stands as an adversary? (6.22)
"O gentle one, you should inform the lord of the earth of these and other matters;
and you should strive in such a way that he does not even remember me. (6.23)
"Even our lack of merit should be mentioned by you to the king;
for through lack of merit, affection is abandoned, and when affection is abandoned, one does not grieve. (6.24)
Having heard these words, Chanda, overwhelmed with grief and distress,
replied with hands joined in reverence and a voice choked with tears.
"O Lord, my heart sinks because of this disposition of yours which brings distress to your kinsmen, like an elephant in the mud of a river. (6.26)
Whose tears would this resolve of yours not cause to flow—even from a heart made of iron, let alone one overwhelmed by affection? (6.27)
Where on one hand is this delicacy, worthy of a celestial chariot and a bed of ease,
and where on the other is the ground of the ascetic grove, covered with the sharp sprouts of darbha grass?
But having heard of your resolve, that this horse was taken away by me—
O Lord, I was compelled to do that by force of destiny alone.
For how could I, being under my own control and knowing this resolve of yours, bring back the horse to cause grief in Kapilavastu? (6.30)
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to abandon this king, who is so affectionate and longing for his son, as an atheist abandons the true Dharma.
And you ought not to forget that second mother, the queen, who was exhausted by the labors of raising you, just as an ungrateful man forgets a kindness received.
You ought not to abandon your queen, who has young sons, who is virtuous, who brings honor to her family, and who is devoted to her husband— just as a eunuch would not forsake attained sovereignty.
[He saw] his praiseworthy son Yashodhara, the best among those who uphold fame and righteousness.
You ought not to abandon this child, just as a gambler does not abandon his most excellent reputation.
Now that you have resolved to renounce both your kin and your kingdom, O Lord, it does not behove you to abandon me; for your feet are my only refuge.
"With my heart burning with grief, I am not able to go to the city,
having abandoned you in the forest, just as Sumantra abandoned Rāghava."
For what indeed will the king say to me when I have gone to the city without you? Out of a desire to appear consistent, what shall I say regarding your inner apartments? (6.37)
As for what you said—that faults should be spoken of even in a king—how could I speak such an untruth of you, who are as faultless as a sage? (6.38)
Even if I were to speak with a heart full of shame and a tongue faltering, who would be able to believe it? (6.39)
For whoever would speak of sharpness in the moon, or believe it, would speak of faults in you, O knower of faults, or believe them. (6.40)
For one who is ever compassionate and constantly sensitive to the suffering of others, the abandonment of those who love him is not fitting; turn back and be gracious to me.

Having heard these words of Chanda, who was overcome by grief, the best of speakers, composed and with supreme fortitude, replied: iti śokābhibhūtasya $ śrutvā chandasya bhāṣitam & svasthaḥ paramayā dhṛtyā % jagāda vadatāṃ varaḥ // 6.42 //
"Abandon this inclination toward separation from me and this torment; for separation is inevitable among embodied beings born into various classes. (6.43)
Although I might not personally abandon my own kin out of affection, I would nevertheless forsake them out of a desire for liberation.
Death will force us, against our will, to abandon one another.
Where am I now for that mother whose efforts were in vain, and where is she for me—she by whom I was held in the womb with great longing and through sufferings? (6.45)
Just as birds, having gathered at a tree, depart once more, so too the meeting of living beings inevitably ends in separation. (6.46)
And having come together, they disperse once again like clouds.
Union and separation—thus have I considered them for living beings.
Since this world departs, deceiving one another in succession,
it is therefore not fitting to feel "mine-ness" toward a meeting that is like a dream.
Trees are separated from their natural leaf-color; when one thing is disjoined from another, how could separation not occur? // 6.49 //
This being so, O gentle one, do not grieve; you may go.
But if your affection still lingers, then having gone, return once more.
And you should say to the people in Kapilavastu: "Do not harbor expectations toward us, nor direct reproaches against us."
Let your affection for him be abandoned, and let his resolve be heard.
"Either he will return quickly after having brought about the destruction of birth and death, or else, failing to achieve his goal and lacking any further effort, he will go to his end. (6.52)
Having heard these words of his, Kanthaka, the best of steeds,
licked his feet with his tongue and shed warm tears.
With his webbed hand, marked with the svastika and the wheel in its center,
the prince touched him and spoke to him like a friend.
"Release your tears, Kanthaka; this noble character has been displayed. Be patient; this labor of yours shall soon become fruitful. (6.55)
Then that steadfast man, having seized from Chandaka’s hand the sharp sword with its jeweled hilt,
drew it from its scabbard— variegated with golden inlays—
like a venomous serpent from its hole.
Having drawn it out—blue as the petal of a blue lotus—he cut off that variegated crown together with the hair;
and as its silken cloth was being scattered in the air, he cast it away like a swan into a lake.
Out of a desire for worship and out of great respect, the denizens of heaven seized that [body] as it was cast away;
and in heaven, the hosts of gods magnified it with divine honors in the proper manner.
Having cast aside his ornaments and his state as a householder’s husband, and having removed the royal turban from his head,
the steadfast prince beheld a variegated silken garment marked with golden swans and longed for the forest attire.
Then a celestial being, pure in nature, having assumed the form of a hunter and perceiving his disposition, approached him wearing saffron robes; the descendant of the Śākya king addressed him.
This auspicious saffron robe, the banner of the seers, is not suited for you, nor indeed is this murderous bow.
Therefore, gentle friend, if you have no attachment to it, give it to me; take this [robe] instead.
The hunter said, "O granter of desires, having gained the trust of the deer with this [decoy] nearby, I slay them at my pleasure."
"But if this object is like Śakra, then—alas!—accept it and bring back this white [robe]. (6.62)
Then, with great joy, he took the wild garment and cast off the fine cloth;
but the hunter, wearing his very own divine form, took that white garment and went to heaven.
Then the prince and the horse-keeper were both astonished as he proceeded in that manner;
moreover, they immediately showed great respect for his forest-dweller’s garment.
Then, having dismissed Chanda with his tearful face, that Great-Souled One— clad in the saffron robe, possessed of steadfastness and wisdom, and bearing a renowned reputation—
went toward the hermitage like the King of Mountains enveloped by evening clouds.
Then, when his master had thus become indifferent to the kingdom and was departing for the penance grove clad in discolored garments,
the horseman threw up his arms, cried out loudly, and fell to the ground.
Looking back again, he wept aloud, embracing the horse Kanthaka with both arms;
then, despairing and lamenting repeatedly, he went toward the city with his body, but not with his heart.
In one place he brooded, and in another he lamented; in one place he stumbled, and in another he fell.
Thus, as he went along, distressed by the power of devotion, he performed many involuntary actions on the road.
Thus ends the sixth canto, named "The Turning Back of Chandaka," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then, having dismissed the weeping Chandaka whose face was bathed in tears, he remained indifferent due to his longing for the forest.
Sarvārthasiddha, surpassing that hermitage with his physical form, entered it as if he were already a perfected one (*siddha*).

That prince, walking with the gait of a lion-king, entered that deer-park like a deer; though deprived of royal splendor, he captivated the eyes of all those in the various stages of life with the beauty of his own body.

For the wheel-bearers, together with their wives, stood with their hands joined in reverence; out of curiosity they gazed upon him who was like Indra, yet they did not move, like draft-animals with their heads half-bowed.
And the brahmins, having gone outside for the sake of sacrificial fuel, returned with fuel, flowers, and purificatory grass in their hands;
though preeminent in austerity and firm in resolve, they went to see him and did not return to their hermitages.
And the peacocks, seeing the dark cloud rising like [the mountain] Udaya, let out joyful cries of *kekā*.
Leaving the young grass, the deer with restless eyes and those who roam among deer stood facing him.
Seeing that lamp of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, blazing like the rising sun,
even though they had already been milked, the cows that yielded the sacrificial oblation flowed with milk, filled with joy.
Could this be one of the eight Vasus, or perhaps one of the two Aśvins who has descended [to earth]? Or could it be Candra?
Upon seeing him, the words of the sages, born of wonder, rose up loudly there: "Ah! (iti).
With a body like that of the bull among the gods, he was like a second light for the world of moving and unmoving beings;
he illuminated the entire forest, like the sun descended by chance.
Then, having been duly honored and invited by those hermits,
he in turn paid homage to those upholders of the Dharma with a voice resembling the rumbling of a rain-cloud.
Desiring liberation, the steadfast one traversed that hermitage— which was crowded with people performing meritorious deeds out of a desire for heaven— while observing their various austerities.

Having observed the various transformations resulting from asceticism among the wealth-holders of austerity there in the penance grove, he, desiring to know the truth, spoke these words to a certain ascetic who was following him: *tapovikārāṃś ca nirīkṣya saumyas tapovane tatra tapodhanānām / tapasvinaṃ kaṃcid anuvrajantaṃ tattvaṃ vijijñāsur idaṃ babhāṣe //* 7.11 // The gentle one, having observed the changes produced by asceticism among those whose wealth is penance in that forest of austerities, spoke this as he followed a certain practitioner of yoga, wishing to discern the reality of things.
"Since this is my first sight of a hermitage today, and because I do not know this rule of dharma, you ought to tell me what your firm resolve is directed toward. (7.12)

Then that twice-born man, whose delight was in asceticism, gradually related to him— the bull among the Śākya bulls and possessed of a bull’s stride— the various distinctions of penance and the fruit of such austerity.

Food that is not from the village, grown in water, leaves, water, fruit, and roots—this is the livelihood of sages according to tradition; yet those various options for asceticism differ according to their specific practices.
Others live by gleaning like birds; some graze on grass like deer;
some subsist together with snakes, having become like anthills [nourished] by the forest breeze. (7.15)
Others subsist on food acquired through the labor of stones; some eat food that has been crushed by their own teeth;
and others, having performed cooking for the sake of another, carry out their purpose only if there is a remnant. (7.16)
Some, with masses of matted locks drenched by water, offer oblations twice into the fire according to the mantras;
others, having plunged into the waters together with fish, dwell there with bodies scarred by turtles.
By such austerities accumulated over time—whether supreme or otherwise—people go to heaven or the world of men;
for by means of a path of suffering they attain happiness. Indeed, they say that the root of dharma is happiness.

Having heard these and other such words of that ascetic, the prince, though he had not yet perceived the ultimate truth, was not fully satisfied; and slowly he spoke this to himself: ity evamādi dvipendravatsaḥ $ śrutvā vacas tasya tapodhanasya & adṛṣṭatattvo 'pi na saṃtutoṣa % śanair idaṃ cātmagataṃ (babhāṣe Cjagāda ) // 7.19 //

Austerity is manifold and consists of suffering, and the fruit of austerity is primarily heaven; all worlds are subject to transformation—truly, this exertion for the sake of the stages of life is but trifling.
And those who, having abandoned their beloveds, wealth, kinsmen, and sense-objects, practice self-restraint for the sake of heaven;
Though they have indeed become detached and desire to depart, they return once more to that very same great bondage, their own forest. (7.21)

He who, through bodily fatigues designated as "austerities," seeks worldly activity for the sake of desire, and fails to examine the defects of cyclic existence—he, by means of suffering, pursues nothing but further suffering. (7.22)
And there is constant fear of death among living beings, yet they strive with effort for rebirth once again.
Since death is certain when there is activity,
one is submerged in that very [activity] from which one is afraid.

For the sake of this world, some enter into weariness; others undergo toil for the sake of heaven. Miserable in their longing for happiness and failing to achieve their goal, alas, the world of living beings falls into misfortune. (7.24)
Indeed, this effort is not at all to be censured, for it is the pursuit of excellence after abandoning what is inferior;
with the same amount of exertion as that of the wise, one should perform that task wherein there is no need to act again.
If bodily suffering here were dharma, then bodily pleasure would be adharma;
yet one attains happiness in the next world through dharma—therefore, it is adharma that bears fruit in this world, while dharma bears fruit there.
For the body proceeds and likewise ceases to act under the control of the mind.
Restraint belongs to the mind alone; therefore, apart from the mind, the body is like a piece of wood.

If merit is desired through purity of food, then even deer possess merit; and so too do those outsiders who, due to the fault of their fate, have turned their backs on the fruits of worldly success. (7.28)
If it is the intention that constitutes the cause of merit in the case of suffering, then surely that same intention should be applied even toward happiness.
Or, if the intention is not an authority regarding happiness, then surely the intention is no more an authority regarding suffering.

Likewise, those who, for the sake of purifying their karma, touch the water thinking it to be a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), even there this satisfaction alone remains in their hearts; for water will not purify their sin. (7.30)
If whatever water is touched by those possessed of virtue is considered a sacred ford on earth, then I regard virtue alone as the true ford; as for the waters, they are undoubtedly just water.
Thus he spoke various words endowed with many arguments, and the sun went to its setting;
then he entered that forest, tranquil through asceticism, where the trees were discolored by the smoke of sacrificial offerings.

With the blazing *agnihotra* fires already lifted up, crowded with sages who had performed their ritual ablutions, and with the chambers of the gods resonant with the sound of muttered prayers, it was like the active workshop of Dharma itself.
There, shining like the moon, he dwelt for several nights examining their ascetic practices;
then, having scrutinized all their penances and concluded that they were insufficient, he departed from that site of asceticism.
Then the hermits followed him with minds captivated by the majesty of his form, as the great seers followed Dharma itself when it was being driven from the land by the barbarians.
Then he beheld those whose wealth was their asceticism, wearing matted hair, bark garments, and rags;
and following after their austerities, he stood at the foot of an auspicious and glorious tree.

Then, having approached and surrounded that best of men, the dwellers of the hermitage stood there; and the eldest among them, with great respect, spoke these words in a gentle and conciliatory tone: 7.37. Then, having approached and surrounded that best of men, the dwellers of the hermitage stood there; and the eldest among them, with great respect, spoke these words in a gentle and conciliatory tone.
When you arrived, the hermitage became as if full; when you departed, it became as if empty.
Therefore, my dear son, you ought not to abandon this [hermitage], just as one who desires to live ought not to abandon his cherished life-force.
For the holy mountain Himavat stands nearby, frequented by Brahman-sages, royal sages, and celestial sages;
indeed, it is through its proximity that the very austerities of those whose wealth is penance become multiplied.
Likewise, on every side were holy places of pilgrimage, which served as stairways to the vault of heaven,
frequented by righteous-souled self-controlled men, as well as by divine seers and great ṛṣis.

Moreover, for the sake of attaining a particular excellence of dharma, it is even more appropriate for the wise man to frequent the northern direction; it is not fitting for him to set foot even a single step toward the south. (7.41)

Now, if you have seen anyone in this forest of asceticism who is inactive, or who has fallen from his duty through confusion, or who is impure—because of whom you have no desire to dwell here—then speak; let your stay be as long as it pleases you.
For these desire you, who are like a treasury of asceticism, as a companion in their penance;
indeed, your dwelling together with Indra-like [Śakra] would bring prosperity to Bṛhaspati.
When this had been said, that chief of the wise, who was the foremost among ascetics,
having made his vow for the destruction of existence, declared his inner state amidst the ascetics.

Because these sages, who uphold the Dharma and are upright in soul, treat guests with such affection as they would their own kin, my supreme joy has been kindled by such manifestations of feeling toward me, and my pride [or: my path] has been humbled. (7.45)
In brief, by these smooth and heart-pleasing words, I feel as if I have been bathed;
and now, the delight of me, who am newly seized by the Dharma, has truly begun to stir once more.
To leave you, who are thus engaged, who are worthy of refuge, and who have shown such great partiality toward me—this causes me as much sorrow as it does for one abandoning his own kinsmen. (7.47)
This dharma of yours leads to heaven, but my desire is for the state beyond rebirth;
it is for this reason that I have no wish to dwell in this forest, for the dharma of cessation has been separated from the dharma of worldly activity.
It is not out of dissatisfaction nor because of any offense by you that I depart from this forest;
for you all are established in the Dharma according to the ancient age, and are indeed like great seers.
Then, having heard the prince’s words— which were truthful, meaningful, very gentle, powerful, and yet full of pride— those ascetics felt a special degree of great respect for him.

There, however, a certain twice-born man—lying upon ashes, tall, with a topknot, dressed in bark garments, with slightly reddish-brown eyes and a long, thin nose, and holding a single water-pot in his hand—spoke these words: 51. There, however, a certain twice-born man—lying upon ashes, tall, with a topknot, dressed in bark garments, with slightly reddish-brown eyes and a long, thin nose, and holding a single water-pot in his hand—spoke these words:

O wise one, your resolve is indeed noble, you who, though young, have perceived the defects in birth; for he alone truly exists whose mind, having rightly deliberated upon heaven and liberation, is set upon liberation.
For those possessed by passion desire to go to heaven by means of sacrifices, austerities, and various observances;
but those endowed with strength of character, having fought against passion as if against an enemy, seek liberation.
If this resolve of yours is firm, then go quickly to Vindhyakoṣṭha;
there dwells that sage Arāḍa, who has obtained the vision of the ultimate good.
Therefore, if you have a genuine inclination, you will hear the path of reality and you will practice it accordingly;
yet, as I perceive this mind of yours, it will cast aside even that [wisdom] once it has discarded its own intellect.
With a prominent nose, large and long eyes, copper-colored lower lips, and white, sharp fangs;
with a thin and red tongue—this face shall indeed drink up the entire ocean of all that is to be known. (7.56)
That profundity of yours which is unfathomable, that radiance, and those marks—
thereby you shall attain the mastership on earth which was attained even by the seers in a former age.
"So be it," the prince replied, and having greeted that company of seers, he departed;
they too, having honored him according to the prescribed rites, entered the ascetic grove of the forest-dwellers.
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Entrance into the Ascetic Grove," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then that groom, dejected at his master having thus departed for the forest, made an effort on the road to restrain his grief; yet even so, his tears could not be checked. (8.1)
The path which he had traveled with that horse by his master’s command in a single night,
he now traversed in eight days while brooding over the separation from his master.
And the horse Kaṇṭhaka, though once full of vigor, moved about with a languid gait; he grew weary in spirit and became devoid of pride.
Though still adorned with his ornaments, he appeared as if stripped of his beauty, bereft of him.
And having turned back toward the ascetic grove, he neighed most piteously again and again;
though possessed by hunger on the road, he neither took pleasure in nor accepted grass or water as he had done before.

Then they gradually approached the city named Kapila, which was bereft of that great-souled one whose very essence was the welfare of the world; it appeared as empty to them as the sky deprived of the sun. (8.5)

Though adorned with lotuses and graced by waters, and further embellished by trees bearing flowers, that very grove of his— resembling a wild forest— did not shine with the city-dwellers whose joy had departed.
Then those two, as if being held back by men wandering in every direction with dejected minds, lacking splendor, and with eyes struck by tears, slowly entered the city which had been bathed in dust.
Thus they both approached. // 8.7 //
And perceiving that those two, their bodies and gait drooping, had departed without the bull of the Śākya clan,
he shed tears.
The people on the road were like citizens when the chariot of the son of Daśaratha arrived in ancient times.
Then, filled with indignation and shedding tears, the people who had followed him along the road spoke to Chandaka:
"Where is the prince, the delighter of the city, the family, and the kingdom?"
"He has been carried off by you!"—thus they pursued him from behind.
Then he said to those devoted people: "I did not abandon the prince;
however, weeping in the lonely forest, I was dismissed by him along with my dress as a householder. (8.10)

Having heard these words of his, those people reached the conclusion that this was indeed most difficult to accomplish; they shed tears from their eyes instead of water, and reproached their own minds for the sake of its fruit.
Then they said: "Let us enter that very forest this very day, where he who possesses the prowess of the king of elephants has gone;
for without him we have no desire to live, just as embodied beings have none when their senses have failed. (8.12)
This city, deserted by him, has become a forest; and that forest, joined with him, has become a city.
Indeed, without him, our city does not shine, just as heaven did not after the slaying of Vṛtra when it was bereft of Indra.
Then, thinking "the prince has turned back," the women crowded toward the rows of windows;
but seeing that the horse's back was empty, they closed the windows again and wailed.
Having entered upon the initiatory rite for the sake of obtaining a son, the lord of men— his mind distressed by both his vow and his grief—
chanted prayers in the temple of the god and performed various rites according to his inclination.
Then, his eyes filled with tears, he took the horse and followed after the horse.
Stricken with grief, he entered the royal palace, as if his lord had been carried off by an enemy in battle.
And as he entered the palace of the lord of men, looking about with eyes streaming with tears,
Kanthaka let out a loud cry with a full-throated sound, as if making known his sorrow to the people.
Then the birds dwelling within the palace and the well-tended horses tethered nearby echoed the sound of that horse, fearing the arrival of the prince.
And the people, deceived by an excess of joy as they drew near to the king’s inner apartments, thought for certain: "Surely the prince is entering, for this horse Kanthaka is neighing. (8.19)
Then, overcome with grief yet longing for a sight of the prince, the women rushed out from their houses in great excitement, flickering with hope like flashes of lightning from an autumn cloud.
With disheveled hair, wearing soiled garments, and faces whose eyes were robbed of their luster by tears, they appeared with unanointed eyes.
The women did not shine with their adornment; deprived of Kṛṣṇā, they were pale as if from the application of collyrium, like stars in the sky reddened at the end of the night.

With feet unadorned by anklets and not yet reddened by copper-colored lac; with faces lacking earrings and necks unbent by the weight of ornaments; with hips naturally full yet devoid of girdles; and with breasts as if robbed of their beauty, being without the cords of jeweled necklaces. (8.22)
(Gazing at them with eyes overwhelmed by tears, she beheld Chandaka and the horse, both devoid of their master and despondent.)
The women wept at his mouth like cows abandoned by their bull in the depths of the forest.
Then Gautamī, the queen of the lord of the earth, filled with tears like a mother cow who has lost her calf, clasped her arms and fell down like a golden plantain tree with trembling leaves.
With their luster gone, their shoulders drooping,
and their arms limp, the other women were as if deprived of consciousness by despair; they neither cried out, nor shed tears, nor sighed, nor did they move, appearing as if they were painted figures.
...as if they were standing [there]. // 8.25 //

Other women, fainting from grief for their husband, drenched their breasts— where the sandalwood paste had vanished— with the streams flowing from their eyes, just as a mountain drenches its rocks with waterfalls.

And with their faces struck by the water from their eyes, O King, that royal residence then shone like a lake whose blooming lotuses are dripping with water when struck by the rain of clouds at the onset of the monsoon.

With their hands— well-rounded, with thick fingers, closely set, unadorned, and with hidden veins— the beautiful women struck their breasts with those lotus-like palms, like wind-swayed creepers striking themselves with their own sprouts.
And those women shone with their breasts raised together, though they were trembling from the blow of his hand;
they were like rivers with pairs of *rathāṅga* birds, shaken by the lotuses tossed by the forest breeze.
Just as they pressed their chests with their hands, so too did they press their hands with their chests;
there, the women, languid with passion, caused mutual pain by pressing their fingertips against each other's breasts.
Then, with eyes reddened by rage and a voice faltering and choked with the bitterness of despair, she spoke with heavy sighs:
Yaśodharā, her breasts heaving and bearing tears of deep sorrow.
"O Chandaka, where has he gone—he who was the fulfillment of my heart's desire—who left me behind while I slept helplessly at night?
Now that you and Kanthaka have returned, yet those three have departed together, my mind trembles. (8.32)

"Having committed this ignoble, unkind, and hostile act against me, O cruel man, why do you weep here today? Restrain your tears and be of contented mind; for your weeping does not correspond to that deed of yours. (8.33)

"With you as a companion—dear, submissive, well-disposed, virtuous, and acting according to the truth—the noble son has departed so as never to return. Rejoice! By good fortune, your labor has borne fruit. (8.34)
Better for a man is a wise enemy than a foolish friend who is unskilled in yoga;
for by you, speaking like a well-wisher yet lacking insight, a great calamity has been brought upon this family.
For these women are indeed pitiable, their ornaments cast aside, their red eyes clouded with incessant tears;
though their husband stands by, equal to the earth of the Himavat mountains, they have lost their splendor like widowed wives.
And these rows of palaces, with their arms of balconies outstretched and the long cries of pigeons clinging to them,
seem to weep bitterly, now separated from him along with the women of the harem.

This horse Kanthaka, too, is surely intent on doing harm to these people in every way; for he has carried away my everything from here while the people were fast asleep at night, like a thief of jewels. (8.38)

When he was indeed capable of enduring even the blows of arrows when they came upon him, let alone the strokes of whips; how then has he gone away out of fear of the fall of a whip, taking with him both my royal fortune and my heart alike? (8.39)
This ignoble creature neighs loudly today as if filling the palace of the king;
yet when my beloved was being led away, that lowest of horses remained utterly mute. (8.40)

For if he had neighed, or had made a sound with his hooves upon the earth while awakening the people, or had produced a loud noise with his jaws, this grief of mine would not have come to pass. (8.41)

Having thus heard these words of the Goddess, which were based on her lamentation and whose syllables were choked by tears, Chandaka, with his face cast down, his voice faltering with sobs, and his hands joined in reverence, slowly uttered this reply: *iti iha devyāḥ paridevitāśrayaṃ niśamya bāṣpavāṣpagrathitākṣaraṃ vacaḥ | adhomukhaḥ sāśrukalaḥ kṛtāñjaliḥ śanair idaṃ chandaka uttaraṃ jagau ||* 8.42 ||

"O Queen, you ought not to reproach Kaṇṭhaka, nor should you direct your anger toward me. Know that we are both entirely without fault; for that god among men, O Queen, has departed like a god. (8.43)
For although I was aware of the king’s command, I have been compelled by certain powers as if by deities;
I have quickly brought this horse here and likewise followed it along the road without experiencing any fatigue.
Even as this noble steed proceeded, he did not touch the earth with the tips of his hooves, which seemed held aloft in mid-air;
likewise, as if by divine power, his face was restrained, he made no sound with his jaws, nor did he neigh.

When the daughter of the king went outside, the gate opened of its own accord; and the nocturnal darkness was rent asunder by her, like the night by the sun—let it be understood that this too was the work of divine destiny. (8.46)

Even though thousands of people in the palace and the city were then vigilant by the command of the king, they did not perceive him, being overcome by sleep; therefore, let it be understood that this too was the work of destiny. (8.47)

Since at that time a garment appropriate for dwelling in the forest was bestowed upon him by a celestial being, and since he wore that crown which had been cast down from heaven— even from this, let it be understood that this is the work of divine destiny.
Therefore, O Queen, you ought not to blame us for his departure;
neither was it my own will nor that of this horse. For he went away escorted by the gods. // 8.49 //

Having thus heard of that wondrous departure of the high-souled one— which was as if filled with many deities— those women were struck with amazement as if their grief had vanished; yet, they experienced a fever of longing for his renunciation.

Then Gautamī, her eyes overflowing with despair, like a distressed osprey whose young have perished, abandoned her fortitude; she wailed aloud, fainted, and with a tear-stained face, spoke thus: 51. Then Gautamī, her eyes swimming with despondency, like a sorrowful osprey that has lost its young, abandoned her composure and cried out; she fainted and, with a face bathed in tears, spoke.
Possessing great waves, soft, dark, and beautiful, they grew forth individually from their roots and were cast about.
Those hairs of his on the earth were fit to encircle the crown of a king's head.
With long arms and the prowess of a lion-king, with eyes like those of a great bull and a radiance brilliant as gold,
with a broad chest and a voice like the sound of a deep drum— even one such as this deserves to dwell in a hermitage.
Surely this earth is unfortunate, for it has not obtained him as its husband—he of noble deeds, unsurpassed.
Having departed from there, that virtuous one indeed [was born]; for such a king is produced by the merits and fortunes of his subjects.

How indeed will those two feet— with toes webbed and well-formed, soft with ankles hidden like the fibers of a lotus stalk, tender as a flower, and marked by the wheels [on the soles]— tread upon the hard ground at the edge of the forest? (8.55)

Accustomed to beds and seats upon the roof of a celestial palace, honored with costly garments, agallochum, and sandalwood—how indeed will that vigorous body endure in the forest when cold, heat, and rain arrive? (8.56)

Proud of his lineage, his being, his strength, his splendor, his learning, his fortune, and his youth, he was accustomed only to giving and not to begging; how will he wander for alms from others? (8.57)
Having slept upon a pure, golden couch at night, being awakened by the sounds of musical instruments—
how indeed will that ascetic of mine sleep today upon the surface of the earth, separated from it only by a portion of a single cloth? (8.58)
Having heard this piteous lament, those women embraced one another with their arms and shed tears from their eyes, like creepers shaken by the wind dropping honey from their flowers.
Then Yaśodharā fell to the ground like a female cakravāka bird separated from her mate;
distressed, she lamented here and there softly, her voice repeatedly choked by sobbing.
If he wishes to practice dharma after abandoning me, his helpless partner in dharma, how can he possess dharma—he who desires to enjoy the fruits of asceticism without a partner in dharma? (8.61)

He surely must not have heard of his ancestors, the former kings beginning with Mahāsudarśa, who retired to the forests together with their wives; for otherwise he would not desire to practice the Dharma in such a manner without me. (8.62)

Nor does he see both husband and wife consecrated together in sacrifices, honored by the Vedic injunctions, equally desiring to enjoy the fruit even in the hereafter; therefore, envy for my merit has arisen in him. (8.63)
Surely that lover of dharma, knowing our mutual quarrels over trifles and jealousies,
has abandoned me in my anger and, fearing no reproach, now seeks to win the Apsarases in the world of Mahendra.

But this thought occurred to me: "What kind of physical beauty do those women there possess, for whose sake he performs austerities in the forest, having abandoned both prosperity and even devotion to me? (8.65)

Indeed, I have no longing for the happiness of heaven, nor is that difficult to attain even for a person possessed of self-control; rather, my heart's desire is this: how might he, who is dear to me, not abandon me either in this world or in the next? (8.66)
If I am so unfortunate as not to behold the long-eyed face of my husband with its pure smile, then this ill-fated Rāhula too shall never again be able to roll about in his father’s lap. (8.67)

"Alas! How cruel and most terrible is the mind of that high-spirited one, whose appearance is so delicate, that he would abandon such an infant son—his own child—who, with his sweet prattle, brings joy even to his enemies! (Bata) // 8.68 //

"Truly, my heart must be made of extremely hard stone, or even of iron, since it does not shatter—even though my husband has gone to the forest like one who is helpless, deprived of his royal splendor, and though he was accustomed to comfort. (8.69)
Thus here the queen, fainting from grief for her husband, wept, brooded, and lamented repeatedly;
for though she was by nature steadfast, in her sorrow that virtuous woman remembered neither fortitude nor shame.
Then, seeing Yaśodharā thus fallen upon the earth, overwhelmed by her lamentations of grief,
the women wailed aloud with tearful faces like great lotuses struck by rain.
Having completed his recitation and performed the auspicious fire-oblation, the king emerged from the temple;
struck by that cry of distress from the people, he trembled like an elephant at the sound of a thunderbolt.
Having observed both Chandaka and Kanthaka, and having heard the firm resolve of his son,
the lord of the earth, struck down by grief, fell like the banner of Indra at the conclusion of a festival.

"O Kaṇṭhaka, after you have performed many dear services for me in battle, you have now done me a great injury; for by this act you have driven my beloved one—who is so fond of virtue—into the forest, casting him away like a foe, even though he is my dearest friend. (8.75)
Therefore, either lead me today to where he is, or go quickly and bring him back again;
for without him I have no life, just as one afflicted by a deep-seated disease has none without the proper medicine.
When Suvarṇaniṣṭhīvin was carried off by Death, it was a most difficult thing that Saṃjaya (or Sṛñjaya) did not die.
But I, though desiring liberation, am like one who does not desire it, for I am without self-mastery now that my son, who delights in the Dharma, has departed. (8.77)

How indeed could the mind of even Manu—the sovereign lord of creatures, the creator of the ten royal seers, the knower of the higher and the lower, whose very self is Vivasvat—not be bewildered when separated from his beloved and virtuous son? (8.78)
I envy that wise son of King Aja, the lord of men and friend of Indra;
for when his son had departed for the forest, he went to heaven, whereas he whose tears were not in vain lived a miserable life.
"Tell me, O blessed one, of that hermitage courtyard where you have taken away my funeral water-offering;
for these breaths of mine, desiring to drink and wishing to go the way of the departed, long for it. (8.80)
Thus, having abandoned his innate fortitude— which, like the earth, endures the suffering born of separation from a son—
the king, overcome by grief for Rāma like Daśaratha, lamented profusely, nearly deprived of consciousness.

Then the aged counselor Matisaciva and the family priest, both endowed with the virtues of sacred learning and discipline, spoke these words appropriately to him—neither with faces of distress nor yet devoid of sorrow:
"Abandon your grief, O best of men; come to steadfastness. You ought not, O wise one, to shed tears like one of base character.
Casting aside royal fortune as if it were a withered garland, many kings on this earth have departed for the forests. (8.83)

Moreover, this disposition of his is fixed; remember the words of the seer Asita from long ago: for he cannot be made to dwell happily for even a moment in heaven, nor in the sovereignty of a universal monarch.
But if, O best of men, effort must indeed be made, then speak quickly so that we may go there; let there first be a manifold battle here between your son and each of those various [opponents]. (8.85)
Then the lord of men commanded them: "Therefore, depart quickly from this very place;
for my heart finds no peace, like that of a forest bird longing for its young. (8.86)
At the king’s command, "It is done," the minister and the domestic priest departed for that forest;
the king also, together with his wives and the women of the court, performed the remaining duties.
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Lamentation of the Inner Apartments," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*.
Then the minister and the domestic priest, spurred by the king with the goad of his tears, departed for that forest with all their might and speed, like two noble steeds urged on by affection. (9.1)

Having reached that hermitage at the appointed time, their fatigue dispelled and accompanied by suitable followers, they cast aside royal splendor and, with humble deportment, approached the very abode of Bhārgava.
Having honored that brahmin according to custom, and having been honored by him in a fitting manner, the two sat down;
and once the descendant of Bhṛgu was seated, they broke off their conversation and spoke of their own business.

"May you know this person as one who has studied under the king born of the Ikṣvāku lineage—a monarch of pure vigor and pure, far-reaching fame—and who is steadfast in both the grasping of sacred learning and the mastery of mantras. (9.4)

The son of that one who was like Indra, who is like Jayanta, has come here desiring to cross over the fear of old age and death; it is for his sake that we two have approached—may the Blessed One understand this. (9.5)
He said to them: "That long-armed prince has indeed arrived, yet he is not yet aware of us;
realizing that this Dharma leads only to rebirth, he has departed toward Arāḍa, seeking liberation. (9.6)
Therefore, having learned the truth from him and having taken leave of that brahmin at that very moment, the two of them—
though weary, yet as if unwearied through devotion to the king— set out immediately for the place where he had gone.
Then, as they were going along,
they saw him, blazing with beauty, though he was destitute of ornaments.
Seated at the foot of a tree by the roadside, he was like the sun that had entered the expanse of a cloud.
Then, leaving his chariot, the family priest approached him together with the mantra-master,
just as the sage Aurvaśeya, accompanied by Vāmadeva, once went to see Rāma dwelling in the forest.
Those two honored the Arhats as Śukra and Aṅgiras honor Mahendra in heaven;
and he in turn honored those two Arhats as Mahendra honors Śukra and Aṅgiras in heaven.
Having been granted permission, those two then sat down on either side of the banner of the Śākya clan;
in his proximity they shone like the two stars of Punarvasu joined with the moon.
To that prince, who was seated at the foot of the tree blazing with splendor, the family priest spoke,
just as Bṛhaspati spoke to Śakra’s son Jayanta when he was seated upon the Pārijāta tree in heaven.
O Prince, when the dart of grief for you had pierced his heart, the king fell to the ground in a swoon; listen now to what he said to you while raining tears from his eyes. (9.13)
I know your resolve regarding the Dharma; I understand this purpose of yours to be unshakable.
Yet, because of your resorting to the forest at an improper time, I am consumed by a fire of grief that is like a blazing flame.

Therefore come, O lover of dharma, for my sake and for the sake of dharma itself, abandon this resolve; for this surging torrent of grief assails me, just as the current of a river strikes its bank. (9.15)

For that very action which wind, sun, fire, and the great thunderbolt exercise upon clouds, water, dry grass, and mountains—that same action grief performs upon us by means of tearing, parching, burning, and cleaving. (9.16)
Therefore, enjoy for now this sovereignty over the earth; you shall go to the forest at the time prescribed by the scriptures.
O you who are not averse to your kin, show consideration for me; for compassion toward all living beings is indeed the Dharma.
And this dharma is not accomplished only in the forest; for even in the city, success is certain for those who strive.
Here, wisdom and effort are the causes; for both the forest and the ascetic’s marks are merely signs of a coward.

Even by householders— kings wearing crowns, with necklaces draped over their shoulders and armlets fastened upon their arms— who were revolving in the very lap of Fortune, the dharma of liberation was attained. (9.19)
The two younger brothers of Dhruva, Bali and Vajrabāhu; Vaibhrāja, Āṣāḍha, and Antideva;
likewise Janaka, the king of Videha; and Druma, the son of Senajit.
Know these kings to be householders disciplined in the dharma that leads to the highest good;
therefore, enjoy both simultaneously— lordship over wealth and the royal glory of lordship over the mind.

For I desire to enter the forest with that very same joy, while closely embracing you, even as you are still wet from the water after your consecration, beholding you with the royal parasol held over you.

"Thus the lord of the earth spoke to you with words whose syllables were choked by tears; having heard this, you ought out of affection to reciprocate his affection for the sake of his welfare. (9.23)
For the King of the Śākyas is sinking in a bottomless ocean of sorrow produced by you, a sea of suffering;
therefore, rescue him who is without a protector, without refuge, and submerged like a ship in the great deep. (9.24)

Having heard that Bhīṣma, born from the womb of the Gaṅgā, and Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu— both of whom performed deeds for the sake of their fathers' pleasure— you too ought to do what is desired by your father.
Regard the queen who raised you as like a loving cow that has lost her calf— she who has not gone toward the quarter favored by Agastya, yet weeps piteously and incessantly in her distress. (9.26)
Like a female swan separated from her mate, like a female elephant abandoned by her bull in the forest—
distressed, though possessing a protector, yet deprived of her lord— you ought to save this bride with your very sight. (9.27)
A single young son, undeserving of suffering, who bore within him a burning anguish.
Deliver that Rāhula from the grief for his kinsmen, as one might release the full moon from the eclipse of Rāhu.
Burning with the fire of grief— fueled by separation from you, with sighs for its smoke and darkness for its flame— he desires the water of your sight; burning within,
he seeks both the inner apartments and the entire city.

That Bodhisattva, a being of perfected virtue who knew all virtues, having heard the words of his domestic priest and reflected for a moment, spoke this humble reply: sa bodhisattvaḥ paripūrṇasattvaḥ $ śrutvā vacas tasya purohitasya & dhyātvā muhūrtaṃ guṇavad guṇajñaḥ % pratyuttaraṃ praśritam ity uvāca // 9.30 //
I understand the affection of parents for their son, especially that which the king bears toward me;
yet, though knowing this, I am forced by necessity to abandon my kin, being terrified of disease, old age, and calamity.
Who indeed would not wish to see their own dear kinsman, were it not for the fact that there is separation from what is beloved?
For even after having existed for a long time...
Therefore, even though he is affectionate, I shall abandon my teacher, for separation from him would be grievous.

"O noble lady, the grief you have spoken of on account of the king does not deserve to be felt by me; for it is not pleasing to me that one should suffer over unions which are like dreams when they end in separation. (9.33)
And thus let your intellect reach a firm conclusion, having observed the manifold course of the world.
Neither a son nor a kinsman is the cause of torment; this suffering has ignorance as its sole cause.
Just as for those traveling on a road,
meeting here [in this world], separation is inevitable for living beings when their time comes.
What wise person indeed would indulge in grief, being deprived of those people promised as kinsmen—though beloved, yet bereft of kin? (9.35)
Having abandoned his own kin here, he deceives them and then departs once more;

having gone there, he goes yet elsewhere. Since people are thus ever-abandoning, what cause is there for attachment to a yogin? (Or: since people are thus ever-leaving, what cause is there for attachment to a yogin? // 9.36 //

Since death follows all living beings for their destruction from the very moment of conception throughout every stage of existence, why has your honor, who loves his son, told me to take refuge in the forest at such an untimely hour? (9.37)
There is no wrong time for attaining sense objects; likewise, the right time is prescribed for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Time drags away the entire world through all its seasons; yet for that excellence which leads to liberation, there is no such thing as "the wrong time."
And as for that kingdom which the king desires me to receive— though it be noble and worthy of my father—
it is not fit for me to accept out of greed, any more than a sick man should take unwholesome food.

How indeed could it be fitting for a wise man to enter into kingship, that abode of delusion, wherein there is agitation, intoxication, and weariness, and where the Dharma is oppressed by the misconduct of others? (9.40)
For sovereignty is like a palace of Jāmbūnada gold set ablaze, like choice food mixed with poison,
and like a lotus pond infested with crocodiles— though beautiful, it is a refuge for calamities.
"Thus, there is neither happiness nor righteousness in kingship;
for just as former lords of men felt revulsion [for it], so too does youth reach its peak amidst unavoidable suffering."
Having abandoned their kingdoms, they went indeed to the forest.
For having eaten grass in the forest,
he embraced supreme contentment as if it were a precious jewel.
It was inhabited by those easily accessible in fortune, yet not by faults that were like invisible black serpents. // 9.43 //
"For it is indeed praiseworthy for kings to abandon their kingdoms and enter the forest out of a desire for the Dharma."
"For one who has broken his vow, it is not fitting to abandon the forest and enter the home. (9.44)
"For what man of courage, born into a noble family,
would enter the forest out of a longing for the Dharma?"
Having cast off his saffron robe and abandoned all shame,
he might even take refuge in the city of Purandara.
For he who, out of greed, delusion, or even fear,
should take back food that has already been vomited.
Whether out of greed, delusion, or even fear, one might abandon sensual desires and then take them up again. (9.46)
And he who, having somehow escaped from a burning house,
should enter it once again.
Having abandoned the life of a householder after perceiving its faults, he might, through delusion, desire to take it up once again. (9.47)
"And as for the scriptural statement that 'kings attained liberation while remaining householders,' this is not so."
Where is the dharma of liberation, which has tranquility as its primary concern, and where is the dharma of kingship, which has punishment as its primary concern? (9.48)
If there is delight in tranquility, the kingdom is lax; if there is intent upon the kingdom, tranquility is destroyed.
For tranquility and sharpness are not compatible, just as cold and heat cannot coexist in water and fire. (9.49)
Or perhaps, out of certainty, those lords of the earth abandoned their kingdoms and attained tranquility.
Or rather, because their senses are restrained, they possess the characteristics of royalty; yet, they harbor the conceit that they have achieved liberation through the life of an ascetic. // 9.50 //
"And let there be peace in their kingdom as it ought to be;
I have not come to the forest out of indecision."
"For having cut the snare known as home and kin, I am liberated and shall not enter it again. (9.51)

Having heard these words spoken by the prince—conformable to his own knowledge of the self, free from longing, reasoned, and powerful—the minister also gave this reply: ity ātmavijñānaguṇānurūpaṃ $ muktaspṛhaṃ hetumad ūrjitaṃ ca & śrutvā narendrātmajam uktavantaṃ % pratyuttaraṃ mantradharo 'py uvāca // 9.52 //
This resolve of yours regarding the performance of dharma [or the best of mantras], is neither improper nor untimely; yet it leads to sorrow [only] after having cut through [all attachments].
For one who desires righteousness, it would not be righteous for you to have a father who has reached old age. (9.53)

Surely your intellect is not very subtle, or perhaps it is unskilled in the matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, since you depart disregarding a visible goal for the sake of a result that remains unseen. (9.54)
Some say that there is rebirth, while others, firm in their resolve, say there is none;
since this matter is thus uncertain, it is fitting to enjoy the prosperity that has presented itself. (9.55)
If there were any further activity, we would delight therein as it occurred; but if there is no further activity beyond this, then the liberation of this world is established without effort. (9.56)

Some say that the next world exists, yet they do not describe the yoga for liberation; for just as heat belongs to fire and fluidity to water, they say that such is the nature inherent in worldly activity. (9.57)

Some describe [things] as arising from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [claiming] that both the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as existence and non-existence, are all inherently so; since this is the case, effort is therefore rendered futile. (9.58)

That the activity of the senses is fixed, as is the pleasantness or unpleasantness of objects, and that one is joined with old age and afflictions—what effort can there be in this? Is it not indeed their very nature? (9.59)
Fire is pacified by water, and the waters cause fire to dry up;
the elements, though distinct when residing within the body, attain unity and sustain the world.

That the state of the being within the womb—the development of hands, feet, belly, back, and head—comes about, and that there is a union between the self and that [body], those who know the truth declare this to be natural (*svābhāvika*). (9.61)
Who creates the sharpness of the thorn, or the diverse nature of beasts and birds?
All this proceeds from its own inherent nature; there is no exercise of will, so how could there be effort? (9.62)

Others say that creation proceeds from God; in that case, what purpose would human effort serve? That very cause which is determined for the world's engagement [in activity] is itself the cause for its cessation. (9.63)
Some say that both the manifestation [of existence] and the destruction of existence are caused by the self alone;
yet they proclaim that manifestation occurs without effort, while the attainment of liberation occurs through effort. (9.64)

A man is born together with these three debts: to his ancestors through progeny, to the seers through the Vedas, and to the gods through sacrifices; for him who has indeed liberation from these, there is liberation. (9.65)
Thus, by this sequence of methods, those who know the truth declare liberation for one who exerts effort;
for even those seeking liberation, though they strive with great exertion, encounter weariness through mere physical endeavor. (9.66)
Therefore, gentle friend, if you have devotion to liberation, follow the prescribed rule according to the right method;
for in this way there will be the attainment of this goal and the destruction of the king’s anguish.
And as for this thought that has arisen in you— the notion that it is a fault to enter a palace from the penance groves—
even there, my dear son, let there be no anxiety; for even the ancients returned to their own homes from the forests.
Even while dwelling in the forest of asceticism, King Ambarīṣa returned to his city when surrounded by his subjects;
likewise, Rāma, having come from the forest of asceticism, protected the earth when it was oppressed by the ignoble.
In the same manner, Drumākṣa, the lord of Śālva, having entered the city with his son from the forest, entered [the city of] Suvapura.
And Antideva, the son of Sankriti, having become a brahmin seer, received glory from the sage Vasiṣṭha.
Thus, those resplendent with the glory of the Dharma, having abandoned the forests, entered their dwellings.
Therefore, there is no fault in returning home from the forest of asceticism for the very purpose of practicing the Dharma.
Then, having heard those words of the minister— which were pleasing and beneficial to the king who was his very eye—
the prince, remaining steadfast in fortitude, spoke these words, which were complete, orderly, unhindered, and measured.
"Whether this exists here or does not exist—this doubt arises from the words of others; I have no certainty in this matter.
Having realized the truth through austerity and tranquility, I shall myself grasp that which is certain herein."
It is not fitting for me to accept a view born of doubt,
which is indistinct and mutually contradictory.
For how could one who relies on another proceed? A person is like a blind man led by a blind guide in the darkness. (9.74)
Although I have not yet perceived the truth, my mind inclines toward the auspicious, even though both the auspicious and the inauspicious appear to me as doubtful;
for the weariness of one whose soul is virtuous, even if in vain, is better than the pleasure of one whose soul is censured, even if that pleasure pertains to the truth.
But seeing that this scripture is inconsistent, know that what has been spoken by the authoritative ones is correct;
and know that their authority consists in their having abandoned faults, for one whose faults are abandoned will not speak untruth. (9.76)

As for what you have said regarding my entering the household life, citing Rāma and others as examples—that is no authority for you; for those whose vows are broken are not sufficient as an authority for the determination of Dharma.
Therefore, even if the sun were to fall to the earth, or even if Mount Himavat were to lose its stability, I,
an ordinary man who has not seen the truth and whose senses are turned toward sense-objects, would never again resort to the household life.
"I would enter even a blazing fire, but I would not enter my home until my purpose was accomplished"—
thus he made his proud vow, and rising as he pleased, he departed, free from worldly attachment.

Then, having heard his firm resolve, both the minister and the brahmin, their faces dejected and filled with tears, followed him in sorrow; yet, unable to proceed further, they slowly returned to the city. (9.80)

Out of affection for him and devotion to the king, the two of them returned with hesitation and stood still; for they were unable either to look upon him on the road—him who was as difficult to gaze upon as the blazing sun—or to leave him, being overcome by his own radiant splendor. (9.81)
Having appointed pure spies to move about in disguise in order to discover the movements of that man of supreme destiny, they departed with difficulty, thinking:
"How shall we go and see the king, who is so longing for his beloved son? (9.82)
Thus ends the ninth canto, named "The Search for the Prince," in the great poem *Buddhacarita*. That prince,
broad-chested and powerful, having left behind those two officials in charge of the sacrificial offerings and mantras,
crossed the Gaṅgā with its surging waves and went to Rājagṛha, the magnificent capital city.
Well-guarded by mountains, adorned, supported, and purified by auspicious ascetics,
he reached that city marked by five peaks, as tranquil as the self-existent Brahmā reaching the vault of heaven.
Beholding his profundity, his vigor, and his radiant form that transcended that of ordinary men,
the people there were then struck with wonder, as if they were looking upon the bull-bannered Śiva himself, who is devoted to the vow of stillness.
Seeing him, he who had gone by another way stood still; he who was standing there on the path followed after;
he who had gone quickly proceeded with steady pace; and whoever was sitting down sprang up.
Some person honored him with both hands; some, having paid respect, saluted him with their heads;
some greeted him with affectionate words;
and no one passed by without having offered him worship.
Seeing him, those dressed in various garbs were struck with shame; their scattered chatter ceased and they fell into silence on the road.
As if in the very presence of Dharma himself, no one harbored an unrighteous thought.
Even while engaged in other activities on the royal highway, the gaze of women or men— fixed with great respect as they beheld that son of a god-like king— found no satiety.
Whether it was his eyebrows, forehead, or face; his eyes, body, hands, or feet; or his gait—whatever anyone beheld of him, there their very gaze became fixed upon that alone. (10.8)
And having seen him— possessing beautiful, curved eyebrows, long eyes, a radiant body, and hands with auspicious webbing— that one in the guise of a monk...
The splendor of Rājagṛha, worthy of being protected by a sovereign, was utterly agitated.
Then Śreṇya, the lord of the Magadha realm,
beheld from his outer palace a vast multitude of people and asked the reason for it; thereupon, a man explained it to him.

"He who was told by the brahmins that he would attain either supreme knowledge or the sovereignty of the earth—he, the son of the Lord of the Śākyas, is now seen by the people as one who has gone forth into the religious life. (10.11)
Then the king, having understood the matter in his mind and having reached a firm resolve, spoke to that very man:
"Let it be known where he is going. Saying "So be it," the man followed after him.
With eyes steady and looking only a yoke’s length ahead, his speech restrained, and his movement slow and controlled,
that best of monks went about for alms, having stilled his limbs and his flickering mind.
Having taken whatever alms he had obtained, he went to a secluded mountain spring;
having eaten there according to the proper rule, he ascended Mount Pāṇḍava.
In that new grove of *lodhra* trees, where the thickets were filled with the cries of peacocks,
that sun among men, clad in saffron robes, shone like the young sun above the mountain of sunrise.

Having observed him there in that manner, the king’s servant reported it to King Śreṇya; and having heard this, the king set out for that place with a modest retinue out of great respect [for the youth]. // 10.16 //

He, whose prowess was equal to that of the Pāṇḍavas, whose stature was like a mountain, who wore a diadem, who moved with the gait of a lion, and who was a lion among men, ascended the best of mountains— Pāṇḍava— as a maned lion ascends a mountain with its flowing mane.

Then, upon that [peak], he saw the Bodhisattva, who had become its very summit, with his senses stilled, seated cross-legged and radiant like the rising moon emerging from a thicket of clouds or a mountain peak. // 10.18 //
With both his physical splendor and his tranquility, he sat there like an emanation of the Dharma;
the king, filled with wonder and humble, approached him just as Śakra approaches the Self-Existent One (Brahmā).
Having approached him according to proper etiquette—that foremost among those who know the rules of conduct—he asked about the equilibrium of his bodily humors;
and he too, with a corresponding gentleness, spoke to the king regarding the health of his mind and his freedom from disease.
Then the king sat down upon a pure stone slab, blue as an elephant’s ear; and having sat near him with his permission, desiring to know his state of mind, he spoke this.

I have the highest affection for your family, which has been inherited through our lineage and is well-tested; since a desire to speak has arisen in me, therefore listen to these words of affection. (10.22)
Your lineage is vast, beginning with the Sun; your age is fresh, and this body of yours is radiant.
Why, then, has your mind turned so prematurely toward the life of a beggar, rather than toward sovereignty?
For this body of yours is worthy of red sandalwood paste, not of contact with saffron robes;
this hand of yours is fit for protecting subjects, not for eating food given by others. (10.24)
Therefore, gentle friend, if you do not desire through force that paternal kingdom out of affection for your father, and if your mind is unable to endure the lapse of due order,
then enjoy half of it.
"Quickly [bring] one from our territory. // 10.25 //
For in this way there would be no crushing of one's own kin, nor would prosperity, even attained through the course of time, find its refuge in tranquility.
Therefore, show me your favor; for the success of the virtuous is augmented by association with the good. // 10.26 //
But now, because of your pride in your lineage, you have no quality of trust toward us; therefore,
having penetrated the arrayed armies with your arrows, seek to conquer the enemies with me as your ally.
Therefore, choose one of these two courses with your intellect; pursue virtue, wealth, and pleasure according to the prescribed rules.
For by deviating from this triad through passion and the like, one suffers ruin both in this world and after death.
They obtain. // 10.28 //
For that pleasure which comes about by crushing both wealth and virtue, and that wealth which comes about by disregarding both virtue and pleasure,
and that virtue which results from the abandonment of both pleasure and wealth— if such an object is desired, it should be entirely renounced.

Therefore, by devoting yourself to the threefold set of goals, make this beauty of yours fruitful; for they say that the complete attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure constitutes the full purpose of human life for men. (10.30)
You ought not to let these two muscular arms, fit for drawing a bow, be rendered fruitless;
for like Māndhātṛ, they are capable of conquering even the three worlds here, let alone this earth alone. (10.31)
"Indeed, I say this out of affection, not from a passion for power nor out of pride; for seeing this mendicant's garb of yours, compassion has arisen within me and tears have come to my eyes. (10.32)

As long as old age has not yet come upon you and overcome this form that is so worthy of your own lineage, enjoy those sensual pleasures, O seeker of the mendicant life; for at the proper time, O lover of dharma, you shall practice dharma.
Indeed, one who is old is able to attain the Dharma; for old age finds no place in the enjoyment of desires.
Therefore, they say that desires are for the young, wealth for the middle-aged, and the Dharma for the elderly. (10.34)

For in this world of living beings, periods of youth are indeed adversaries to both dharma and artha; though they are being guarded, they are difficult to restrain, since sensual desires carry one away along that path. (10.35)
The faculties of the wise, though worn out by age, become reflective, steadfast, and intent on remaining still;
they become characterized by tranquility with little effort, both through the very nature of their decline and through shame. (10.36)

And so, having transcended youth— which is fickle, centered on sense objects, heedless, impatient, short-sighted, and full of many deceits— they breathe a sigh of relief as if having crossed a wilderness.
Therefore, let this youth—which is unsteady, fickle, and prone to negligence—pass away for now;
for the early age of desire cannot be protected from the senses. (10.38)
Moreover, if your desire is indeed for dharma, then perform sacrifice; this is the family tradition.
For by means of sacrifices, even Indra, having ascended to the vault of heaven, went to the vault of heaven.
With their arms adorned by golden armlets and their variegated crowns radiant with the light of jeweled lamps,
those royal seers indeed attained that goal which the great seers reached through arduous toil by means of sacrifices.
Thus spoke the Lord of Magadha,
who shone as he spoke correctly, like Indra himself.
Having heard that, the prince did not waver, like Mount Kailāsa with its many variegated peaks.
Thus ends the tenth canto, named "The Visit to Śreṇya," in the great poem *Buddhacarita* composed by Aśvaghoṣa.

Then, having been addressed in this way with an unfavorable proposal by the lord of Magadha through the mouth of a friend, the son of Śuddhodana—composed, unshaken, and pure in lineage and integrity—spoke these words: 11.1 //
It is no wonder that such conduct should be prescribed for you, born as you are in the great lineage of the lion-crested Ikṣvākus;
for this is the pure way of life for one who desires friends and acts toward his circle of friends with such integrity.
Affection toward the unworthy does not endure, following one's own family tradition, just as prosperity does not remain with the faint-hearted;
however, the virtuous increase that very affection which was established by their ancestors through a succession of friendly acts. (11.3)

Those men in this world who become partners in action with their friends during times of hardship for them—I consider those alone to be true friends by my own judgment; for who would not be a friend to one who is healthy and in a state of prosperity? (11.4)

And thus, those who, having acquired wealth in this world, employ it for the sake of friends and the Dharma—their riches have attained their true essence; they do not cause remorse at the end when they are lost. (11.5)

"O King, because of my friendship and my nobility toward you—having considered this very resolve of yours regarding me—I shall conciliate you through that very friendship; I would say nothing else in response to this. (11.6)

Having recognized the fear of old age and death, I have sought refuge in this Dharma out of a desire for liberation; having abandoned my dear kinsmen with tearful faces, how much more so have I abandoned sensual pleasures, which are the causes of impurity. // 11.7 //
I do not fear venomous serpents, nor indeed thunderbolts falling from the sky, nor fires fanned by the wind; such is my fear of these very objects of the senses. // 11.8 //

For sensual desires are impermanent, thieves of virtue and purpose; empty and like illusions in this world, they delude the minds of men even when merely longed for—how much more so when they are possessed? (11.9)

For those overcome by sensual desires find no peace, whether in the triple heaven or indeed in the world of mortals; for there is no satisfaction for one who thirsts for desires, just as there is none for fire aided by the wind when fed with fuel. // 11.10 //
In this world, there is no misfortune equal to sensual desires, yet through delusion people remain attached to them;
knowing this truth, what wise man, fearing misfortune, would himself desire such a calamity? (11.11)
Even after obtaining the earth clothed by the ocean, they still desire to conquer the further shore of the great sea;
there is no satisfaction for the world through its desires, just as there is none for the ocean from the waters falling into it.
Even after the god had rained down a shower of gold, and even after he had conquered all four continents as well as the oceans,
and even after attaining half of Śakra’s throne, Māndhātṛ remained unsated with sense-objects. // 11.13 //
Even after enjoying the sovereignty of the gods in heaven while Śatakratu had fled out of fear of Vṛtra,
Nahuṣa— having, out of pride, even made the great seers carry him about— fell, unsated in his desires.

And King Aiḍa, having entered the third heaven and brought that goddess Urvaśī under his control, fell into ruin because he was insatiable for sensual pleasures; out of greed, he desired to seize gold from the sages.

Who could place their trust in those who, having overthrown Mahendra as Nahuṣa and then Indra from the position of Mahendra, returned once more to Nahuṣa—whether in heaven or on earth—amidst objects of sense that are agitated by the fluctuations of fortune? (11.16)

Even sages—clothed in bark, subsisting on roots, fruits, and water, and bearing matted locks as long as serpents—were broken by them; for what man would seek out those enemies known as "desire"? (11.17)

Even for those on whose account Ugrāyudha, though wielding a formidable weapon, met his death at Bhīṣma’s hands, even the mere thought of them leads to an inauspicious end; how much more so, then, for those who act according to their own whims and live without restraint? (11.18)

Perceiving that the gratification found in sense-objects is slight, that it results in an increase of fetters and only insatiability, and considering the reproach of the virtuous and the certainty of evil—who would rashly take up that which is called desire, which is in truth poison? (11.19)

Having heard of the suffering of those afflicted by labors such as agriculture, and of those possessed by [worldly] dharmas who are driven by desire, as well as the composure of those who have no longing for sensual pleasures, it is fitting for self-possessed men to abandon desires. (11.20)

One should know that the attainment of desires is a calamity for one who longs for them, for when desires are fulfilled, one falls into intoxication; through intoxication, one performs what should not be done and neglects what should be done, whereby, being ruined, one falls into an evil rebirth. (11.21)

Who here, being wise and self-possessed, would take delight in these sensual pleasures—which, though acquired with effort and guarded with care, depart once again after having deceived one—regarding them as mere borrowed goods? (11.22)

Having sought them out and grasped them, one becomes thirsty for more; not abandoning those things which lead to suffering as one wanders about, what man of self-mastery could find delight in those sensual pleasures that are like a grass torch in this world? (11.23)

Those who, lacking self-mastery, are bitten by these [desires] in their hearts meet with destruction and find no peace; what person of self-control could find delight in those desires which resemble angry and fierce serpents? (11.24)

Like dogs afflicted by hunger, who do not become satiated even after eating, what person of self-control could find delight in those sensual pleasures which are like a skeleton of decayed bones? // 11.25 //
For those who produce suffering because they are common property to kings, thieves, water, and fire—
what man of self-mastery could find delight in such sensual pleasures, which are like meat thrown away?

For what self-possessed person could find delight in those sensual pleasures—which are like a slaughterhouse—wherein those who dwell abide surrounded by calamity, both from the enemy and even from their own kin? (11.27)
Those who attempt to overstep them meet with downfall on the mountain, in the forest, in the waters, and in the ocean.
In these sensual pleasures, which are like the fruits at the very tops of trees, what self-possessed person could find delight?

What person of self-mastery could find delight in those sensual pleasures— which are like the enjoyments of a dream and, though attained through intense and various efforts, perish here in an instant? // 11.29 //

What self-possessed person would find delight in those sensual pleasures, which are like pits of glowing coals— pleasures that do not bring peace even when honored, nor when increased, nor when protected? (11.30)
For whose sake the Kurus, the Vṛṣṇis, the Andhakas, and the Daṇḍakas met their destruction—
[those who were like] the butcher’s knives and spears.
What person of self-possession could find delight in those sensual pleasures, which are like wooden statues? (11.31)

For what purpose the two Asuras, Sunda and Upasunda, perished, having been driven by mutual enmity—for what pleasure could a self-possessed man find in those desires that cause the dissolution of friendship? (11.32)
For whose sake they cast themselves here into water, into fire, or among carnivorous beasts, their consciousness blinded by desire; who indeed would do so out of compassion?
What person of self-mastery could find delight in those desires, which are like enemies and inherently inauspicious? (11.33)
For the sake of desire, the ignorant man—blinded by passion—acts miserably; he encounters suffering such as slaughter and imprisonment.
Wretched with his hopes for the sake of desire, the poor soul undergoes death and exhaustion.
The world of living beings (jīvaloka). // 11.34 //
For deer are lured to their slaughter by songs; moths fall into the fire for the sake of its form;
and the fish, seeking bait, swallows the iron hook. Therefore, the objects of the senses result in misfortune.
If the thought should arise that "desires are indeed enjoyments," then upon careful examination,
there are no enjoyments whatsoever to be found.
For in the world, things such as clothing and other material goods should be understood as merely remedies for suffering. (11.36)
For water is desired for the quenching of thirst, and food likewise for the destruction of hunger;
a house for protection against wind, sun, and rain; and clothing for the covering of the privities and for warding off the cold. (11.37)

Likewise, a bed is for the sake of dispelling sleep; a vehicle is for the destruction of fatigue from the road; a seat is for the purpose of resting in one place; and bathing is for the sake of cleanliness, health, and strength. (11.38)
Therefore, objects are not enjoyments for living beings, but rather they serve as the means for remedying suffering.
What wise man, engaged in the performance of a remedy, would accept [the premise] that "I am enjoying pleasures"?

He who, being scorched by the burning heat of bile, should determine that a cooling treatment is an "enjoyment," and who, engaged in the method of counteracting suffering, should apply the designation of "enjoyment" to sensual pleasures—he indeed would be acting thus. (11.40)
Since there is uncertainty regarding sensual pleasures, for this reason as well I have no notion of enjoyment toward them;
for those very same things that bestow pleasure bring about suffering once again.
Heavy garments and likewise aloe-wood are for comfort in the cold,
but for discomfort in the heat.
The rays of the moon and sandalwood paste bring pleasure in the heat, but cause pain in the cold.
