Since all pairs of opposites, beginning with loss and gain, are attached to everyone in this world, for this reason too there is no one anywhere on earth who is exclusively happy, nor anyone who is exclusively miserable. (11.43)
Having seen that the nature of pleasure and pain is intermingled— considering both sovereignty and servitude to be equal—
the king indeed never laughs, nor does the slave ever grieve. (11.44)

Since authority is greater in kingship, for that very reason the sufferings of a king are great; for a king is like a wooden stake of attachment, and he undergoes exhaustion for the sake of the world. (11.45)

If a king places his trust in a generous friend who possesses many faults, he perishes; yet even if he does not place such trust, what indeed is the happiness of a king who remains in a state of constant apprehension? (11.46)
And when, even after conquering the entire earth, only a single city is seen fit for residence, and within that city,
only a single palace is to be inhabited— surely the status of a king is labor for the sake of others.

Even for the king, there was but a single pair of garments; likewise, food in just sufficient measure to suppress hunger, and a bed as well as a single seat—only these; all other luxuries served only for the intoxication of the monarch.
If this fruit is desired for the sake of contentment, I have contentment even without a kingdom;
and when contentment exists for a man in this world, are not all distinctions indeed without distinction? (11.49)
Therefore, I am not to be enticed back toward sensual desires, for I have set out upon the secure and auspicious path;
yet, remembering our friendship, speak to me again and again, saying: "Truly, keep your vow."
For it was not out of resentment that I entered the forest, nor because my crown has been struck down by the arrows of an enemy;
nor do I harbor a longing for those who possess superior fruits, since I do not accept this word of yours.

He who, having released a furious, venomous serpent, would resolve to seize it again; or who, having cast away a blazing grass-torch that is inherently burning, would seek to embrace it once more—he alone might pursue sensual desires. (11.52)
He who, being sighted, should envy the blind; he who, being free, should envy the bound; and he who, being wealthy, should envy the destitute.
And he, with a healthy mind, should feel compassion for one whose mind is deranged and who is devoted to sense objects.
One who subsists on alms is not to be pitied, for he is accomplished and desires to cross over the fear of old age and death;
he for whom there is the highest happiness of peace in this world, and whose sufferings in the next world have been shut away. (11.54)

Even while abiding in great prosperity, one who is overcome by craving is to be pitied— he who does not attain the bliss of peace in this world and is instead seized by sufferings in the life hereafter. (11.55)
It is indeed worthy of you to speak thus, consistent with your character, conduct, and lineage;
and it is likewise fitting for me to fulfill my vow, consistent with my own character, conduct, and lineage.
For I, pierced by the arrow of saṃsāra, have gone forth, desiring to attain peace.
I would not wish to obtain even the untroubled sovereignty in the triple heaven, much less among human beings.

"O King, as for what you have told me—that the complete pursuit of the three aims of life is the supreme goal of man—I see this rather as a misfortune; for the triad of aims is perishable and does not bring true satisfaction. (11.58)
But in that state where there is neither old age, nor fear, nor illness, nor birth, nor cessation, nor mental afflictions;
I consider that alone to be the supreme human goal, wherein there is no further repeated action.

As for what you said—that old age should be guarded against because youth undergoes transformation—this is an uncertainty, for it is seen to be fickle: even old age can be unsteady, and youth can possess steadfastness.
And when Death, expert in his own work, drags the world helplessly through all stages of life;
When the time of destruction is uncertain, how can a wise man seeking peace wait for old age? (11.61)

When the hunter Death stands ready—armed with old age, scattering his arrows of disease, and relying on the bow of misfortune—piercing the deer of living beings that dwell in the forest of destiny, what hope can there be for the prolongation of life? (11.62)

Therefore, whether one is young, old, or even a child, one ought to act with such haste in this world that the conduct of a righteous person—one who has disciplined the self or whose nature is compassionate—may result either in active engagement or in renunciation. (11.63)

As for what you said—that I should perform for the sake of dharma the sacrificial rites appropriate to my lineage, which yield desired and radiant fruits—I pay homage to such sacrifices; for I do not desire that happiness which is sought by inflicting suffering upon another. (11.64)

For it is not fitting for one who is compassionate by nature to slay another who is helpless out of a desire for the fruit [of sacrifice], even if the fruit of the ritual were eternal; yet having performed it, what would he gain that is of a perishable nature? (11.65)

Even if there were no other dharma than through vows, moral conduct, or the pacification of the mind, one still ought not to perform a sacrifice in which the stated fruit consists of the slaughter of another being. (11.66)

Even in this world, whatever happiness proceeds for a man who stands by inflicting injury upon others—that too is undesirable to the compassionate and wise; how much more so, alas, that which is not seen in another existence? (11.67)
Nor am I to be enticed toward the pursuit of fruits; O King, my mind finds no delight in worldly existences.
For all worldly activities are as fickle as creepers struck by the rain from a cloud, for they are unstable in every respect.

Having come here from that place out of a desire to see the sage Arāḍa, who teaches liberation, I shall depart this very day, O King; may you be well. Please forgive my words, which were harsh due to their focus on the reality of tranquility. (69)

Protect us like Indra, O Lord of Gods; protect us constantly like the Sun; protect us with your virtues; protect us here for our ultimate welfare; protect the earth; protect the life-force; protect the noble sons through the Āryas; and, O King, protect your royal splendors and your own dharma.

Just as a bird, at the end of its life-span, enters the fire— the enemy of cold— to cast off its body, so too, at this juncture, enter the fire— the enemy of enemies and the destroyer of foes— to liberate your mind.
With palms joined in reverence, the king spoke with longing: "May you obtain whatever you desire without hindrance;
and when you have achieved this fulfillment of your purpose in due time, you must likewise show me your favor."

Having firmly promised "So be it" to the king, he then went to the Vaiśvantara hermitage; and the king, filled with wonder upon seeing him departing as a wandering mendicant, also set out for his city, Giri-vraja. (Or: and traveling, he reached this mountain. // 11.73 //
Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Reproach of Sensual Pleasures," in the great poem *Buddhacarita* composed by Aśvaghoṣa.
Then, the moon of the Ikṣvāku lineage [approached] the sage who dwells in tranquility.
He went to the hermitage of Arāḍa, as if filling it with his own physical splendor.
Having been addressed with a loud "Welcome! by that man of the Kālāma clan even from afar as soon as he saw him, he drew near.
Having questioned each other according to custom regarding their physical well-being, the two sat down on a pure spot upon seats made of wood, which were sacred and capable of bestowing virility.
To that prince as he sat, that best of sages spoke,
as if drinking him in with his two eyes wide with great respect.
It is known to me, O gentle one, how you have departed from your home,
having severed the bond consisting of affection, like a proud elephant breaking its tether.
In every way, your mind is indeed steadfast and wise,
since you have come here having abandoned royal fortune like a creeper bearing poisonous fruit.
It is no wonder that kings in their advanced years retired to the forest,
having bestowed their royal splendor upon their offspring like a garland already worn and discarded.
This thought of mine is a marvel: that you, while still in the bloom of youth, have reached this state without having enjoyed royal splendor, yet remain within the range of the senses.
Therefore, since you are the supreme vessel for understanding this Dharma,
take hold of the raft of knowledge and quickly cross the ocean of suffering. (12.9)
Even though a disciple has become learned, the scripture is expounded [only] in due time.
On account of your profundity and your resolve, you are not to be scrutinized by me.
Having understood these words of Arāḍa, that bull among men [the lord of men]...
He became exceedingly pleased and spoke this reply.
That this supreme cheerfulness of yours exists even though you are dispassionate—
by this, though my own purpose remains unfulfilled, I now feel as if it has been fulfilled.
For I consider your sight to be like one desiring to see light, like one wishing to travel seeking a guide, and like one wishing to cross over needing a boat. (12.13)
Therefore, you ought to speak that which is to be spoken, if you deem it fit,
so that he may be completely liberated from old age, death, and disease.
Thus Ārāḍa, impelled by the very majesty of the prince,
briefly set forth the conclusion of his own treatise.
Listen, O best of listeners, to this our established doctrine: how the cycle of existence comes to be, and likewise how it ceases to be. // 12.16 //
Nature and its transformations, birth, death, and likewise old age—this is what is called "existence" (sattva); O you of steadfast being, go beyond that.

In this context, however, O you who are skilled in the knowledge of nature (*prakṛti*), know that what is called "nature" consists of the five elements, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) itself. (12.18)
Understand that "modification" refers to the intellect, the sense objects, and the senses; as well as the hands, the feet, speech, the anus, the generative organ, and likewise the mind. (12.19)
From the discernment of this field, he is designated as the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña);
and those who contemplate the self describe the self as the "knower of the field. (12.20)
It is recorded here that Kapila, together with his disciples, was "the Awakened" (*pratibuddha*); however, Prajāpati, along with his son, is said here to be "the Unawakened" (*apratibuddha*). (12.21)
That which is born, grows old,
is afflicted, and dies should be known as the manifest; the unmanifest, however, is the opposite.
Ignorance, karma, and craving are to be known as the causes of saṃsāra;
whatever being remains within this triad does not transcend it. (12.23)
From misconception, from egoism, from doubt, from confusion, from lack of distinction, from lack of means, from attachment, and from falling away. // 12.24 //
In that context, what is called "misconception" (vipratyaya) functions erroneously; it performs an action in a contrary manner and conceives of what is to be thought in another way. (12.25)
"I speak," "I know," "I go," "I stand"— thus does the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) function here, O you who are free from ego-sense.
But he who perceives entities that are non-doubtful as being doubtful through their state of unity—like a lump of clay, free from doubt—he is here called "doubt. (12.27)
"That which is I, that very same thing is this mind, the intellect, and action; and whatever is this group, that am I"—this is what is called "complete identification" (*abhisaṃplava*). // 12.28 //

He who knows the lack of distinction between the awakened and the unawakened, and understands the lack of distinction among the constituent natures (prakṛtis), is known as one who perceives the non-distinct. // 12.29 //
Salutations, the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, sprinkling with water, ritual ablutions, and the like—these are known by the wise as non-means, O Knower of Means. (12.30)
By means of which [actions], the one of dull intellect becomes attached through mind, speech, intellect, and deeds.
Non-attachment toward sense objects—that is what is known as "attachment. (12.31)
That suffering which one conceives of as "this is mine" or "I am this" should be known as a downfall, by which one is cast down into saṃsāra. (12.32)
Thus, the wise man indeed strives against ignorance, which has five joints.
Darkness, delusion, great delusion, and likewise the two types of gloom.
In this context, know that indolence is darkness (*tamas*), and delusion (*moha*) is both death and birth;
let it be understood that great delusion (*mahāmoha*) is indeed passion (*kāma*). (12.34)
Because even great beings become utterly deluded herein, therefore, O mighty-armed one, this is known as "Great Delusion" (mahāmoha). // 12.35 //
They declare that *tāmisra* is indeed non-anger, while they designate *krodha* as *andhatāmisra*; and they proclaim that *aviṣāda* is [the opposite of] despondency.
Bound by this fivefold ignorance, the fool is immersed again and again in births within saṃsāra, which is filled with suffering. (12.37)
Thinking "I am the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and indeed the agent of action," one comes to such a notion and wanders about in saṃsāra. (12.38)
O wise one, by these causes, the stream of birth and death proceeds.
"You ought to understand that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of a fruit. 12.39 //
In this regard, one who desires liberation should understand with right understanding these four: the awakened and the unawakened, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest. (12.40)
Having understood this fourfold [set] exactly as it is, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), indeed,
having abandoned the state of coming and going, attains the imperishable state.
For this purpose, the Brahmins in the world who are exponents of the supreme Brahman practice celibacy here and cause other Brahmins to dwell [with them]. (12.42)
Having heard these words of that sage, the prince asked about the means as well as the ultimate state.
"You ought to explain this practice of the holy life—how it is practiced, to what extent, where, and the ultimate limit of this Dharma. (12.44)
Thus Ārāḍa, according to the scriptures, explained that very dharma to him again by another method, concisely and with its meaning made perfectly clear. (12.45)
Having first abandoned his home and adopted the mark of a mendicant,
he lives having taken up a morality that is extensive in its proper conduct.
Relying upon supreme contentment with whatever he may obtain from wherever it comes,
the wise and skillful man, free from the pairs of opposites, dwells in a secluded abode.
Then, seeing danger in passion and supreme auspiciousness in dispassion,
he restrains the collection of his senses and strives for the tranquility of the mind.
Then, secluded from sensual desires and likewise from ill-will and the rest, he attains the first dhyāna, born of seclusion and accompanied by applied thought (vitarka). 12.49.
Having attained that meditative bliss and dwelling upon it again and again, the foolish person is carried away by the acquisition of an unprecedented happiness. (12.50)
By such tranquility as this, which censures desire and hatred,
one attains the world of Brahmā, being deprived [of higher goals] by mere contentment.
Having recognized that discursive thoughts cause agitation of the mind, the wise man attains a meditative absorption free from them, endowed with joy and bliss.
He who, being carried away by that affection, does not perceive any distinction,
attains a radiant station among the Ābhāsvara gods.
But he who withdraws the mind from that joy and pleasure attains the third dhyāna, which is bliss devoid of joy.
But he who is immersed in that bliss and makes no effort for further distinction attains a bliss in common with the Śubhakṛtsna deities.
Having attained such happiness, he who does not become attached, but remains equanimous—
He attains the fourth dhyāna, which is free from both pleasure and pain.
In that regard, some who are conceited resolve upon this, thinking, "This is liberation."
Because of the relinquishing of pleasure and pain, and because of the non-activity of the mind.
But those who investigate with great wisdom declare that the fruit of this meditation is equal to the gods of the Bṛhatphala heaven; it is called Bṛhatkāla, Bṛhat, and Bṛhatphala.
Having emerged from that concentration and having seen the defects of embodied beings,
the wise man ascends to knowledge for the sake of turning away from the body.
Then, having abandoned that meditation and being resolved upon something more distinguished, he—
being wise— becomes dispassionate even toward form, just as one is toward sensual pleasures.
First imagining the cavities that exist within this body, he then resolves upon space even within solid substances. (12.61)
But another wise person, having contracted the self— which is like space— right then and there, [proceeds].
Seeing the distinction at the end, he attains realization.

But another, skilled in the internal states, having turned himself away from [unwholesome] states by means of his own self, perceives that "nothing exists" and is thus known as one who dwells in the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanya). // 12.63 //
Then, like a reed from its sheath or a bird from its cage,
the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) having emerged from the body is designated as "liberated."
This is that supreme Brahman, signless, eternal, and imperishable;
that which the wise who know reality call liberation.
"Thus have both the means and liberation been shown to you by me; if they are understood, and if there is a desire for them, let them be practiced accordingly. (12.66)
Jaigīṣavya, Janaka, the aged Parāśara, and others who seek liberation, having reached this path, have indeed been liberated. (12.67)
Having thus received those words of his and having reflected upon them, he—
impelled by the power of past causes— spoke this reply.

I have heard this subtle knowledge, which becomes increasingly auspicious at each successive stage; yet because it does not involve the renunciation of this Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) within the non-fields (*akṣetra*), I understand it to be incomplete.

For even though I consider the Knower of the Field to be liberated from both the transformations and the primal nature, I still regard him as possessing the quality of procreation and indeed the quality of a seed.
For even if the self is imagined to be pure and liberated, it will become unliberated again due to the continued existence of causal conditions. (12.71)

"Just as a seed does not sprout due to the absence of the proper season, soil, and water, but does sprout through various such conditions; even so, in my view, that [defilement] is likewise understood. // 12.72 //
"Furthermore, liberation is conceived as resulting from the abandonment of karma, ignorance, and craving;
yet that ultimate abandonment is not possible if a self exists. (12.73)
Having abandoned each of these three, a further distinction is perceived;
yet wherever the self remains established, there these three exist in a subtle form.
Because the faults are subtle, because the mind is inactive,
and because the lifespan is long, liberation is indeed postulated.
This abandonment of egoism that is being postulated is impossible; as long as a self exists, there can be no abandonment of egoism.
Furthermore, as long as he is not liberated from number and the rest, he cannot be devoid of qualities;
therefore, in the absence of the state of being devoid of qualities, his liberation is not predicated.
For there is no discernment between the possessor of qualities and the qualities themselves;
indeed, fire is never perceived apart from its form and heat. (12.78)
Before the body there could not have been an embodied being, and likewise before the qualities there could not have been a possessor of qualities;
therefore, having been liberated from the very beginning, the embodied one is bound again.
The knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is either bodiless, and thus either conscious or indeed unconscious;
if he were conscious, he would have an object of knowledge, and as long as there is an object of knowledge, he is not liberated. (12.80)
Furthermore, it is established for you that [the self] is ignorant; what is the use of a postulated self?
For even without a self, ignorance is well-established, as in the case of wood or a wall.
Since renunciation is considered virtuous insofar as it proceeds further and further,
I consider the complete fulfillment of one's purpose to consist in the total relinquishment of everything.
Having thus understood the doctrine of Arāḍa, he was not satisfied;
realizing it to be incomplete, he then departed from there.
Then, desiring to hear about further distinctions, he went to the hermitage of Udraka;
yet, because of that [teacher's] grasping at a self, he did not accept even his teaching.
Having recognized the fault in both perception and non-perception, the sage Udraka attained the state beyond nothingness— a realm characterized by neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because perception and non-perception are subtle with respect to their object, and beyond that there is neither non-perception nor even perception, therefore he has no longing for that state. (12.86)

And because the intellect remains fixed right there, not wandering elsewhere— being subtle and unrefined— therefore, in that state, there is neither a lack of perception nor the presence of perception.
And because the world returns again even after attaining that [state],
the Bodhisattva, desiring the supreme goal, therefore abandoned Udraka.
Then, having left that hermitage, seeking the highest good and firm in his resolve,
he repaired to the hermitage known as a city belonging to the royal seer Gaya.
Then, on the pure bank of the Nairañjanā, the Sage of pure prowess,
delighting in solitary dwelling, made his abode in that secluded place.
Before that, he beheld five monks who were practitioners of austerity and vows, yet who were agitated by the power of the five senses. (12.91)
And seeing him there, those monks who sought liberation approached him,
just as the objects of the senses approach a lord who possesses wealth and health acquired through merit.
He was being honored by them, who were bowed low and following him with humility, their forms bent in reverence.
By his disciples, who remained under his control, as the fickle senses remain under the mind.
Thinking, "This may be the means for bringing an end to birth and death," he then began difficult ascetic practices, beginning with fasting.
Performing many rules of fasting that are difficult for men to practice, he brought about emaciation of his own body for six years, desiring to attain the state of tranquility.
And at meal times, desiring to reach the further shore of the shoreless saṃsāra, he sustained himself with single grains of kola, śakola, sesame, and rice.
Whatever wasting of his body was brought about by that austerity,
that very same thing was produced again for him as an even greater increase of vital energy.
Though emaciated, he possessed undiminished fame and splendor, and brought joy to the eyes of others.
Like the moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight of autumn for the water-lilies.
Though reduced to skin and bone, with all his fat, flesh, and blood entirely consumed, he shone like the ocean— his depth undiminished even in his emaciation.
Then the sage, whose body was distressed in vain by his evident and arduous austerities, being fearful of worldly existence, formed this thought out of a desire for Buddhahood: (12.100)
This dharma does not lead to dispassion, nor to awakening, nor to liberation;
that fixed method which was attained by me at the foot of the Jambu tree then remains constant.
And since this cannot be attained by one who is weak, he, filled with earnest resolve, reflected further on this for the sake of increasing his bodily strength: (12.102)
Exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, with a mind unwell due to weariness, how could one who is not at peace obtain the fruit attainable only through the mind? (12.103)
Nirvāṇa is properly attained by the constant gratification of the senses;
through the state of having the senses fully gratified, the mind attains well-being.
For one whose mind is healthy and serene, meditative concentration (samādhi) arises;
for one whose mind is endowed with concentration, the practice of meditation (dhyāna-yoga) proceeds. // 12.105 //
Through the practice of meditation, those qualities are attained by which that supreme, immortal state—peaceful, ageless, and difficult to reach—is obtained. (12.106)
Therefore, he reached the certainty that this means is rooted in food; thus, the steadfast one of immeasurable intellect resolved his mind upon the destruction of food. (12.107)
Having bathed at the bank of the Nairañjanā, he, emaciated, slowly emerged from the water,
as the trees on the shore gave him a hand by bowing down their branch-tips out of devotion.
Then Nandabalā, the daughter of the cowherd chief, impelled by the deities and with joy arising in her heart, arrived there.
With her arms radiant with white conch shells and clad in a dark blue garment,
she was like the Yamunā, the best of rivers, whose dark waters are adorned with garlands of foam.
With her faith increased by that act of devotion, her joy blossoming like lotus-eyes,
she bowed her head to him and caused him to accept the milk-rice.
Having enjoyed her and thereby obtained the fruit of his birth,
he became capable of attaining awakening, with his six sense-faculties fully satisfied.
The Sage, whose form was fully nourished and endowed with great fame, [proceeded] together with his retinue.
He alone bore the splendor and fortitude of both the moon and the ocean; bearing the sole burden of fortitude, he shone like the moon and the ocean combined.
Perceiving that he had turned back, the five monks abandoned him.
Like a wise man, he regarded himself as liberated from the five elements.
Then, with Resolve as his companion, having traversed the ground covered in young grass,
he proceeded to the foot of the Aśvattha tree, firm in his determination for enlightenment.

Then, at that time, Kāla, the best of serpents, possessing the prowess of a lordly elephant, awakened by the incomparable sound of the Great Sage’s footsteps and having reached the certainty of his attainment of awakening, uttered this hymn of praise.
Since the earth seems to groan again and again as it is pressed by your feet, O Sage,
and since your radiance shines like the sun, you will surely enjoy the desired fruit this very day.
Just as the rows of blue jays wheeling in the sky circumambulate you to the right, O lotus-eyed one,
and just as gentle breezes blow from the heavens, you will surely become a Buddha this very day.
Then, having been praised by the best of serpents and having taken pure grass from a mower,
he who had made his vow sat down for the sake of awakening, taking refuge at the foot of a great, pure tree.
Then he assumed that supreme, unshakable cross-legged posture, coiled like the body of a sleeping serpent, thinking:
"I shall not break this seat upon the earth until I have achieved my purpose; I will not depart until I have accomplished what is to be done."
Then the dwellers of heaven experienced incomparable joy;
neither the herds of deer nor the birds uttered any cries.
The forest trees, though struck by the wind, did not rustle when the Blessed One, whose mind was firm, had taken his seat.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, named "The Vision of Ārāḍa," in the *Buddhacarita*, a great poem composed by Aśvaghoṣa.
When that great seer, born of a lineage of royal sages, had made his vow for liberation—
When he had sat down there, the world rejoiced, but Māra, the enemy of the true Dharma, trembled with fear.

Him whom they call Kāmadeva in the world, who possesses variegated weapons and flower-arrows, and who is the sovereign lord of the movement of desire—it is he whom they declare to be Māra, the enemy of liberation. (13.2)
His sons— Vibhrama, Harṣa, and Darpa— and his three daughters, Arati, Prīti, and Tṛṣṇā,
questioned him regarding the perturbation of his mind; he spoke these words to them both.
That sage, wearing the armor of resolve, drawing the bow of courage with the arrow of wisdom, remains desirous of conquering my sense-objects; therefore, this is the sorrow of my mind.
For if he should surpass me and depart, proclaiming the path to liberation to the world,
then this domain of mine today will become empty, like that of the King of Videha when he fell from his conduct.
Therefore, while he has not yet attained the eye of wisdom and remains within my domain,
I shall go to break his vow, just as the swollen current of a river breaks a dam.

Then, taking up a bow made of flowers and five arrows that cause delusion— the arrows of worldly infatuation— he approached the foot of the Ashvattha tree with his son, bringing unrest to the minds of all living beings.

Then Māra, fixing his left hand on the tip of his weapon and playing with an arrow, spoke thus to the Sage who sat there in perfect tranquility, desiring to cross to the further shore of the ocean of existence: 8. "Having fixed his left hand on the tip of his weapon and playing with an arrow, Māra spoke this to the Sage who sat there in perfect tranquility, desiring to cross to the further shore of the ocean of existence."
Arise, O Kṣatriya, you who fear death! Practice your own duty;
abandon the dharma of liberation with your arrows!
And having disciplined the world through sacrifices, may you attain the station of Vāsava.
For this path is glorious for one to depart upon, which was trodden by the most ancient lords of men;
it is not fitting for one born into the great lineage of royal seers to resort to this ignoble life of begging.
Now, if you do not rise [from this], O resolute one, remain firm and do not abandon your vow;
for here is that very same arrow raised by me, which was once loosed at Śūrpaka, the enemy of the fish.
And he, though the grandson of Soma, became somehow bewildered when touched by him;
and he became Śantanu.
When the age has declined, he is no longer independent; alas, how much more so any other weakling! (13.12)
Therefore, rise quickly and regain your senses;
for here stands this arrow, licking its lips, which I do not discharge even at the cakravāka birds who are devoted to their mates and fond of pleasure. (13.13)
Although addressed in this manner, when the Śākya sage remained unperturbed and did not even shift his seat,
Māra then discharged an arrow at him, placing his daughters and sons before him.

But even when that arrow was released, he paid it no heed nor did he waver from his steadfastness; seeing him thus, Māra despaired and, overcome with anxiety, spoke softly: tasmiṃs tu (bāṇe Cvāṇe ) api sa vipramukte $ cakāra nāsthāṃ na dhṛteś cacāla & dṛṣṭvā tathainaṃ viṣasāda māraś % cintāparītaś ca śanair jagāda // 13.15 //

"He by whom even the god Śambhu was pierced and shaken when he struck the daughter of the Mountain King—this man does not even think of that very arrow; could it be that he is heartless? No, it is not that this is no arrow. (13.16)

Therefore, he does not deserve the flower-arrow [of the God of Love], nor exhilaration, nor even the service of Rati; he deserves only to be terrified, threatened, and beaten by the remaining hosts of ungentle spirits. (13.17)
Then Māra, desiring to create an obstacle for Śākyamuni’s peace, recalled his own army;
and his followers, taking various forms, surrounded him with arrows.
Holding in their hands drums, spears, clubs, and swords. // 13.18 //
Some had the faces of boars, fish, horses, donkeys, and camels; others had the faces of tigers, bears, lions, and elephants.
Some had but one eye, some many mouths, some three heads, some pendulous bellies, and others were pot-bellied.
Some had no knees and were stuck to their thighs; others had knees like jars, and some were armed with fangs while others were armed with claws;
some had skulls for faces and headless trunks for hands.
And those with many forms, with broken halves of their faces, and with enormous mouths.
Reddish-brown like ash,
variegated with red drops, holding skull-topped staffs in their hands, and possessing hair that is greenish-yellow and smoky-grey;
Some wore long garlands, some had ears like those of elephants, some were clad in skins, and others were entirely naked.
Some had white faces and green bodies, others were copper-colored, smoky, tawny, or black;
likewise, some had serpents draped as upper garments upon their arms, while others wore girdles crowded with loudly ringing bells.
Some were the size of palm trees, grasping spears; others were the size of children with terrifying fangs;
some had the faces of sheep and the eyes of birds; others had the faces of cats and the bodies of men.
With disheveled hair, wearing topknots or half-shaven heads, clad in red garments or entwined with ropes,
they had faces both exultant and frowning; some were robbing others of their splendor, while others were captivating the mind.
Some, as they went along, leaped about violently; others likewise sprang up toward one another;
some played while moving through the air, and others moved upon the tops of trees.
One danced while whirling a trident; another roared, dragging a mace that flashed with light;
another bellowed with joy like a bull; and yet another blazed forth from the hair on his body.
Such hosts of spirits stood surrounding the foot of that Bodhi tree on all sides;
both desiring to seize him and desiring to slay him, they remained there, fulfilling their master’s command.
Beholding that time of battle between Māra and the Bull of the Śākyas during the first watch of the night,
the sky did not shine, the earth trembled, and the quarters of the horizon blazed forth with a roar.
A wind blew from every direction with increased force; the stars did not shine, nor did the moon appear;
the night spread forth even deeper darkness, and all the oceans were violently agitated.
The mountain-dwelling nāgas, devoted to the Dharma and unable to endure the obstacle posed to the Great Sage, cast their eyes wide with rage toward Māra; they hissed and yawned.
But the divine sages, whose abodes are pure, have set out for the sake of accomplishing the true Dharma.
They felt compassion for Māra in their minds, yet because of their state of detachment, they did not fall into anger.

Beholding that foot of the Bodhi tree strewn with that host of Māra, whose nature is violence, those beings whose very soul is Dharma and who long for the liberation of the world raised a cry of "Alas! from the sky.
But seeing that host of Māra standing there, intent on disrupting the rite of that Great Seer who was well-versed in the Dharma, [the seer remained unmoved].
He was neither agitated nor did he undergo any change of state, sitting there like a lion in the midst of cattle.
Then Māra commanded his surging army of spirits for the sake of terrifying him;
thereupon, that host of his, each by its own power, set its mind upon breaking his fortitude.

Some stood there, indeed, causing terror by their very appearance: with tongues hanging down in many ways as they moved, with sharp-pointed and fierce fangs, with eyes like circles of fire, with gaping mouths, and with ears fixed like spikes. // 13.35 //
Though they stood there in such a state, terrible in both appearance and disposition,
the great seer was neither shaken nor alarmed; he played with them as one would play with unruly children.
Then, with eyes rolling in rage, someone raised his mace against him;
but his arm, together with the mace, was instantly paralyzed, just as Indra’s arm with the thunderbolt was once paralyzed in the past.
Some, having lifted up rocks and trees, were not at all able to hurl them at the Sage;
they fell down just so, with their trees and rocks, like the foothills of the Vindhya mountains shattered by a thunderbolt.
Some, having leaped up into the sky, released stones, trees, and battle-axes;
these remained suspended in the very heavens and did not fall, like the multicolored feet of clouds at twilight.
Another hurled at him a blazing mass of straw as large as a mountain peak; yet, the moment it was released, while still suspended in the sky, it shattered into a hundred pieces through his power.
Like the sun risen in full blaze, another emitted a great shower of glowing coals from his mouth,
like Mount Meru ablaze at the end of an aeon, scattering fragments of its golden caverns.
That shower of burning coals with sparks, being scattered at the foot of the Bodhi tree,
became a rain of red lotus petals through the power of the Great Seer’s dwelling in loving-kindness.
Though struck by such afflictions of body and mind and by those very scorching heats,
the Śākya Sage did not stir from his seat, as if embracing his own resolve as a kinsman. (13.43)
Then others vomited forth serpents from their mouths, as if from withered trees; yet,
as if bound by spells, they hissed not in his presence, nor did they move.
Then other massive clouds appeared, accompanied by lightning and the fierce roar of thunderbolts;
they released a rain of stones upon that tree, which instead became a beautiful rain of flowers.
Then, when an arrow was fixed upon another’s bow, it blazed right there and did not fly forth;
like the wrath of an impatient man who lacks self-mastery, it burned within himself even as he was being urged on.
But five arrows, released by another, remained suspended in the sky and did not fall upon the Sage;
they were like the five senses of an examiner who fears cyclic existence when it comes to the engagement with sense objects.
Another, enraged and desiring to slay him, rushed forward toward the great seer wielding a mace; failing to reach his goal,
he fell helpless, just as the world falls into harmful vices.
A woman, dark as a cloud and holding a skull in her hand, was indeed [sent] to cause delusion of mind for the great seer.
He wandered there without restraint and did not remain still, like the intellect of a fickle person amidst the scriptures.
A certain man, having fixed his blazing eye upon him as if wishing to consume him with the fire of his gaze like a venomous serpent,
beheld that seer sitting right there— like one whose soul is possessed by desire beholding the highest good being taught.
Another, lifting a heavy rock, labored in vain with his efforts frustrated,
like one desiring to attain the Dharma— which is reached through knowledge and meditative concentration— by means of physical exhaustion alone.
Others, with the forms of hyenas and lions, let out great, loud roars;
at which all creatures fled in every direction, thinking that the sky, struck by a thunderbolt, was bursting asunder.
Deer and elephants,
uttering cries of distress, fled and hid themselves;
and during that night, birds flew about from all directions, crying out as if it were day, overcome with grief.
But by those such shrieks of theirs, even though all living beings were made to tremble,
the sage was neither terrified nor did he shrink away, just as Garuḍa is unmoved by the cries of crows.
The more the Sage did not fear those terrifying hosts of the assembly,
the more Māra, the enemy of those who uphold the Dharma, sank down under the weight of both grief and rage.

Then a certain being of invisible form, a distinguished spirit dwelling in the sky, having seen Māra— who was free from enmity yet enraged by his malice toward the Seer— spoke to him in a loud voice: bhūtaṃ tataḥ kiṃcid adṛśyarūpaṃ $ viśiṣṭa(rūpaṃ Crūpaṃ ) gaganastham eva & dṛṣṭvarṣaye drugdham avairaruṣṭaṃ % māraṃ babhāṣe mahatā svareṇa // 13.56 //
O Māra, you ought not to labor in vain; abandon your murderous nature and go to find peace.
For he cannot be shaken by you, any more than the great mountain Meru can be moved by the wind.
Fire might even abandon its nature of heat, water its fluidity, and earth its stability;
but he, who has accumulated meritorious karma over many kalpas, would never abandon this resolve.
For his resolve, his prowess, his splendor, and his compassion for living beings—
without attaining the ultimate truth, he will not rise up, just as the thousand-rayed sun does not rise without having destroyed the darkness.

For by rubbing wood one obtains fire, and by digging the earth one finds water; for the persevering man there is nothing that cannot be accomplished—indeed, nothing is impossible for him—if everything is done with persistence, according to right method, and with skill.
Taking pity on that world, which is afflicted and beset by diseases such as passion and the like, he is the great physician.
This man, who is undergoing hardships for the sake of the medicine of knowledge, does not deserve to meet with an obstacle.

When the world has been led astray by many wrong paths, it is not right to disturb that guide who seeks the true path with such toil— just as one would not disturb a good guide when a caravan has lost its way.

While beings have perished in great darkness, this lamp of knowledge is being made; it is not right for the Noble One to extinguish it, just as a lamp being lit in the dark [should not be put out]. (13.63)

And seeing the world submerged in the great flood consisting of saṃsāra, unable to find the further shore—if someone were to set out to rescue it, who could possibly think ill of that noble one? (Or rather, who could lead him astray? 13.64.

The tree of knowledge, which bestows the fruit of Dharma—having patience for its fibers, firmness for its deep roots, conduct for its flowers, and mindfulness and wisdom for its branches—is growing; it truly does not deserve to be uprooted. (13.65)

It is not fitting for you to desire to harm him whose mind is intent on liberating his subjects from the firm bonds of delusion that bind them, especially since he is weary from striving for the sake of releasing the world from its fetters.
"For today is the fixed time for those deeds which he has performed for the sake of awakening;
it is fitting that he sits here in this very place, just as the sages of old did. (13.67)
For this is the navel of the earth’s surface, endowed with the entire supreme splendor;
there is indeed no other region of the earth that could endure the power of his concentration, which is the domain of his welfare.
Therefore, do not grieve; attain peace. O Māra, let there be no pride in you because of your greatness.

It is not fit to place confidence in fortune, for it is unstable; why do you feel wonder at a station that stands on a shifting footing? (Or rather: why do you take pride in a station that is transient? 13.69.

Then, having heard those words of the great sage and observing his unshakable composure, Māra departed with a dejected mind and his efforts frustrated— those arrows by which the world is struck down in its heart.

Then that army of his fled in all directions, its joy vanished and its labor rendered fruitless, with its stones, brushwood, and trees scattered; it was like an enemy host whose protector has been slain by a foe.
When the flower-bannered god of love had been conquered and his faction defeated, and the Great Seer— free from passion and having overcome all darkness— was triumphant,
the sky shone with the moon like a smiling young woman; and a fragrant rain of flowers, pregnant with water, fell down.

Nevertheless, when the Evil One had been defeated and departed, the quarters of the sky grew serene, the maker of night shone forth, showers of flowers fell from the heavens to the earth, and the night gleamed like a woman cleansed of all stain. // 13.73 //
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, named "The Victory over Māra," in the *Buddhacarita*, a great poem composed by Aśvaghoṣa.
Then, having conquered the host of Māra through both fortitude and tranquility,
he who was skilled in meditation, desiring to discern the ultimate truth, entered into deep reflection.
Having attained supreme mastery over all the methods of meditation,
he recalled the succession of his previous births during the first watch of the night.
"In that place I was named so-and-so; having passed away from there, I have come here"—thus he remembered thousands of births as if experiencing them once again. (14.3)
Remembering birth and death within those various rebirths, he,
whose very nature was compassion, then felt compassion for all sentient beings.
Having abandoned one's own kin here and performing rites elsewhere once more,
this world indeed wanders like a wheel, utterly without protection.
As he was thus recollecting this, that self-controlled man reached the certain conclusion:
"Saṃsāra is as devoid of essence as the core of a plantain tree. (14.6)
But when the second watch had arrived, he of peerless prowess obtained the divine eye—
the supreme eye— being the best among all who possess sight.
Then, with that divine and purified eye,
he beheld the entire world as if in a stainless mirror.
As he beheld the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their inferior and superior karma, his compassionate nature increased.
"These living beings of evil deeds go to a miserable rebirth;
these others of virtuous deeds are established in the triple heaven. (14.10)
Having been reborn in this most dreadful and terrifying hell, these beings are, alas, miserably tormented by manifold sufferings. (14.11)
Some are made to drink molten iron as hot as fire;
others, screaming, are impaled upon red-hot iron pillars.
Some are cooked like flour in iron cauldrons with their faces turned downward; others are piteously burned in blazing heaps of glowing coals. (14.13)
Some are devoured by fierce dogs with sharp iron fangs;
others are seized by bold crows made of iron, as it were, with iron beaks.
Some, exhausted by the heat and longing for cool shade, enter the dark forest of sword-leaves as if they were bound there.
Some, their arms bound fast, are split like wood with axes; yet even in such suffering they do not perish, for their life-breaths are sustained by their karma.
Whatever action was performed with the thought, "May there be happiness," for the sake of the cessation of suffering—
the fruit of that is this very suffering which is now experienced by those who are powerless.
Having performed unwholesome deeds for the sake of happiness, those who are now thus intensely suffering—does that past relish bring even the slightest bit of happiness to them now? (14.18)
The foul deed that was committed with laughter by those of defiled minds is experienced with wailing when the time for its ripening arrives. (14.19)
If those who have committed evil deeds were to see the fruit of their actions,
they would vomit hot blood, as if struck in their vital organs.
For a wise person, dwelling together with ignoble people is considered a far greater hardship than even the physical sufferings of those in the hells.

These other miserable beings, born through various deeds arising from the stirrings of the mind, have been reborn in the manifold animal realm.
Where, for the sake of their flesh, skin, hair, or teeth, even out of enmity or intoxication, pitiable beings are slaughtered while their own kinsmen look on. (14.22)
Though unable and powerless, tormented by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, they are driven like oxen and horses, their bodies wounded by the goad.
And those who have become elephants are driven by the weak, even though they are stronger;
their heads tormented by goads, they are struck with feet and heels.
Even though other sufferings exist, there is suffering here in particular because of mutual conflict and because of total dependence on others. (14.25)
For those dwelling in the sky are oppressed by those who dwell in the sky; those dwelling in the water by those who move in the water;
and those dwelling on land by those situated on land—each being overcome by their respective counterparts.
Thus have they been reborn here in the world of the ancestors, which is devoid of light; with their minds overcome by stinginess, they experience their miserable fruit.
With mouths like the eye of a needle and bellies like mountains, those who share in suffering are tormented by the pains born of hunger and thirst. (14.28)
Even when they have transcended their [former] intentions, yet are sustained by their own past actions, these beings do not obtain even discarded filth to eat. // 14.29 //
If a person were to know such a fruit of stinginess,
they would give away even their own limbs in every way, like Śibi. // 14.30 //
These other beings, having reached a prison resembling hell—a foul pool known as the womb—take birth among humans and experience suffering. (14.31)
